# My Claude Code

Release 8.17.0. A local multi-provider LLM proxy, model router and control plane for AI coding agents.

Licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 or later (AGPL-3.0-or-later), or a commercial licence by negotiation.

## My Claude Code: local LLM gateway for coding agents
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/

One address in front of every model and every coding agent

My Claude Code is a local multi-provider proxy, model router and control plane for AI coding agents. Point Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI and the rest at one address on your machine, and manage providers, keys, fallback chains, reasoning, budgets, web search and cost in one place. Your models, your keys, your machine. It is a Claude Code proxy first, and a proxy for every other coding agent beside it.

What it is

MCC is a local LLM gateway, proxy and model router for AI coding agents. Instead of configuring providers, API keys, models, fallbacks, reasoning effort and spend tracking separately inside every coding tool you use, you point those tools at one address on your own machine and manage the routing layer once.

It runs entirely on your machine. It has no telemetry and phones home to nothing; its only outbound traffic goes to the providers you configure. Your keys stay in one .env you own.

60

provider cards in the README's provider table

4

protocol doors behind one router

905

test files in the repository

8.17.0

the release this site documents

Why it exists

A coding agent is a client. It speaks one protocol, expects one model name, and has no idea which provider answered. MCC makes that separation real: the agent keeps its own interface, while the model behind it can be a cloud API, a subscription, a gateway or a local server, with a fallback chain behind every route.

That separation is what makes the rest possible. A request can be re-routed when a model rate-limits. A key can be rotated without touching the agent's configuration. Reasoning effort can be translated once into each provider's own dialect. Every request can be priced at the moment it is logged, with the source of each number recorded beside it.

Who it is for

It is for the developer who runs more than one agent and more than one provider: Claude Code on one project, Codex on another, a local model for a private repository, and a paid API for the work that needs it. Each of those tools has its own configuration file, its own key store and its own idea of what a model is called. MCC gives them one address and one place to change the answer.

It is also for the person who wants to know what a routing decision actually did. A fallback that fired, a key that was benched, a price that no source could state: each is a row in the log, not a story reconstructed from a terminal. That is why the analytics pages are as detailed as the settings pages.

It is not a managed service. MCC runs on your machine, with your keys, and there is no account to create and no dashboard outside your own address.

The request path

Four protocol doors reach the same router. Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode, Crush, Kimi Code and Qwen Code speak Anthropic Messages; Codex speaks OpenAI Responses; Cline, Goose, Aider and every OpenAI-shaped SDK speak Chat Completions; Gemini CLI and Antigravity speak Google's Gemini API. The router resolves the requested tier to a real model, applies your reasoning and output-budget settings, picks a healthy credential and walks the fallback chain when a provider fails. The reply is translated back into the protocol the agent asked in, and the whole exchange is priced and logged once on its way out.

Four protocol doors, one router and one executor.

A diagram showing Claude Code, Codex, Cline and Gemini CLI entering four protocol doors that all meet one shared router and executor.

What you can do with it

Model tiers and fallback chains

Route Fable, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku traffic to a model you chose, with an ordered stand-in list behind every tier.

Reasoning and budgets

One effort setting translated into each provider's dialect, plus output ceilings, deadlines and a per-model calculator.

Providers and credential health

Cloud, subscription and local backends, multi-key rotation, per-key health and learned provider facts.

Agent support

Launchers for the CLI agents, Configure and Undo for desktop apps, generated model catalogues and request attribution.

Analytics and cost provenance

A searchable request log, rollups and latency, and cost that keeps reported and estimated figures apart.

Native web search and fetch

Claude Code's web_search and web_fetch tools fulfilled at the proxy, with a chain of search providers and a keyless fallback.

Discord and Telegram sessions

Run managed coding-agent sessions from a chat, with voice-note transcription and stop and clear commands.

Media routing

Image, speech, transcription and video endpoints over rails with the chat engine's retry, key and proxy rules.

Platform and packaging

Windows, macOS and Linux, a desktop app and tray, one update path and npm and PyPI packaging.

The command line

Launchers, the headless mcc-apps controls and the installer's own flags.

The local dashboard

Every setting above, local-only, at one address, with its own appearance, updates and docs.

A control plane, not a wrapper

The dashboard is the part you can see. It opens on a Get Started checklist and then gets out of the way. The Providers page is one searchable card per provider. Model Config is one rail per tier with its real fallback chain. Analytics is a request log and everything computed from it. Each of those pages reads and writes the same .env the server reads, so the dashboard and the file never disagree.

Six tier rails, each with its primary model and its numbered fallback chain. A struck-through row is paused and is never tried.

The request log is the other half of the control plane. Every completed request is logged, priced and searchable across prompt, reply, reasoning and tool calls. A fallback that fired, a key that was benched, a reasoning field a host refused: each is a row with its reason, not a story you have to reconstruct from a terminal.

Analytics: stored requests, success rate, fallback share and token totals, with an all-time strip that keeps counting after stored rows roll over.

Install it in one line

Every install route ends at the same server, the same dashboard and the same configuration directory. The one-liners install uv and a managed Python 3.14 if they are missing, verify the release wheel's SHA-256 and put every mcc-* command on your PATH.

Linux, macOS or WSL

curl -fsSL "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FiredMosquito831/my-claude-code/main/scripts/install.sh" | sh

Windows Command Prompt and PowerShell have their own one-liners, and there is a native desktop app for each platform. After any install, close and reopen your terminal: the installer adds ~/.local/bin to your PATH, and a shell that was already open cannot see it.

Then: run mcc-server , open http://127.0.0.1:8082/admin , add one provider key on Providers , set your tiers on Model Config , and launch an agent with mcc-claude .

## About My Claude Code
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/about/

The project and its history

My Claude Code is an independent open-source project maintained by FiredMosquito831. It is a local routing layer for AI coding agents, and it says what it does without claiming more. This page is About My Claude Code: who maintains the project, what state it is in, and what it does not claim.

Status

The current release is 8.17.0. The project is active: providers, routing rules and protocol surfaces change release by release, and the documentation is updated beside the code. The repository is public, the test suite is in the repository, and the issue tracker is the place to report a defect. This site documents the behaviour the repository verifies; where a source disagrees with itself, the discrepancy is noted in the site's own record rather than smoothed over.

8.17.0

current release

905

test files

60

provider cards

AGPL

or commercial

How it got here

This repository began as a fork of an earlier MIT-licensed project by Ali Khokhar (Alishahryar1) and became a standalone project on 2026-09-05. Every commit, branch and tag carried across unchanged: the Git history here is byte-for-byte the history it always had, and every release from v4.x onward is present with its original notes and assets. The upstream author and the MIT notice are credited in the licence file.

GitHub pull requests are database records rather than Git objects, so they could not travel with the code. They are preserved as documents instead: the repository's history/pull-requests/ directory holds all 284 of them with their descriptions, conversations, reviews and commit lists, plus the raw API payloads. Each one names the commit it merged as, and that commit is in this repository's history.

Two consequences are worth knowing. Pull request numbers written into old commit subjects refer to those archived records rather than to anything in this repository. And release publication dates all read 2026-09-05, because the API cannot backdate them; the tag and commit dates are the real ones.

What was inherited

The model-routing infrastructure inherited from the upstream project by Ali Khokhar stays under its original MIT license, and substantial portions of it remain in this project. The repository's licence file carries the full terms, including the MIT notice. The rest of the project is dual-licensed under the AGPL or a commercial licence, which the licence page sets out exactly.

What this site is

A product site, not a documentation reader. It is generated from the repository by a deterministic builder and committed alongside the documentation source, which it never modifies. Every capability page carries a claims list, every number is either computed from the repository or recorded against the command that produced it, and the screenshots are the product's own captures, reviewed and redacted on copies before publication.

The site is deliberately plain in one respect: it loads no external font, no content delivery network, no analytics and no embed. It reads as text with JavaScript disabled. That is a choice about trust, not a limitation of the tooling.

Contact

The project's GitHub profile is the contact channel: github.com/FiredMosquito831 . A defect or a feature request goes to the repository's issues. A vulnerability goes to the private security route named in the repository's policy, never to a public issue.

## Architecture: how the local LLM gateway works
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/architecture/

How the system is put together

MCC is a local proxy, a set of launchers and an optional messaging bridge, built from eight packages with one dependency rule. This page is the map; the six pages after it go into the machinery a request actually touches. Read together, they are the LLM gateway architecture: the doors, the routing ladder, the credential layer, the request log and the cost model.

The repository documents its own architecture in a long, maintained file. This page condenses the parts that explain the behaviour you can see: why one address can serve four protocols, why a credential can be judged without judging the model, and why a request is priced once rather than reconstructed later.

Three runtime surfaces

The HTTP proxy. A FastAPI application exposes the Anthropic Messages, OpenAI Responses, Chat Completions and Gemini routes, the health and model-listing routes, and the admin surface.

The CLI launchers. Wrapper entrypoints prepare a coding agent, or a managed session, to target the local proxy.

The messaging bridge. Optional Discord or Telegram adapters turn chat messages into managed client sessions.

Four protocol doors, one router and one executor.

A diagram of the four client protocols meeting one shared router and executor.

All three surfaces end at the same proxy. A chat-driven request and a terminal-driven one are the same kind of request once they reach the router, which is why routing, keys, cost and health behave identically whichever surface sent them.

Eight packages, one dependency rule

The installable wheel is eight packages. config and core are dependency leaves and import nothing first-party. application depends on those two. messaging depends on core . providers depends on application , config and core . The api depends on the same three. The cli depends on config and core . The runtime is the composition root and depends on everything else. There is one deliberate exception: the CLI delegates server construction to the runtime's bootstrap.

The package graph and its allowed edges. An import-boundary test derives and checks it.

A diagram of eight packages: config and core as leaves, application, messaging, providers, api and cli above them, and runtime as the composition root.

An import-boundary contract derives every static production edge with one AST scanner and checks the package matrix, the exact exception, facade ownership and lazy optional imports. The resulting graph must stay acyclic. The same contract rejects untyped provider collaborators and private provider access from helper modules. This is the structural reason the boundaries hold: they are tested, not merely documented.

One request, from door to log

A request enters a route, passes proxy authentication, acquires the current provider generation, is validated and routed, is shaped by reasoning and budget settings, and is executed against one provider at a time. The reply is translated back into the client's protocol. The whole exchange is priced and logged once. The next pages take that apart.

What the pipeline produces: one request's route attempts, the reasoning it sent and the fallback that answered.

Where the state lives

One configuration directory holds one .env and the documents beside it. The request log is a local SQLite database, with a search index and a prompt chunk store beside it. Catalogue snapshots, OAuth stores, proxy chains and learned facts are separate documents, so a settings save does not rewrite a credential and a credential refresh does not rewrite a setting.

The loop the architecture is built to support: serve, log, inspect, change, re-measure.

A six-step loop from a served request through the log and analytics to a change and a re-measurement.

The six deep pages

The request path

Ingress, auth, routing, the provider lease and the commit boundary of a streamed reply.

Provider routing

How a tier becomes a model, how the chain is walked, and how a platform narrows what a stream can say.

Credential health

The rotation engine, the three health signals and the two ladders that can bench a key.

Cost provenance

The pricing ladder, the rung stored beside each number, and why reported and estimated never merge.

Data and storage

The configuration home, the request log, the search index and the chunk store.

Security model

The principles the boundary is built on: local by default, a token once it leaves, narrow egress.

Testing and CI

Deterministic tests cover API routes, configuration, provider conversion, upstream adapters, streaming contracts, messaging, CLI adapters, import boundaries and provider-catalogue contracts. Local and live smoke tests live apart, so a test that launches a subprocess or touches a real service cannot be mistaken for a unit test. The repository holds 905 test files, and the CI workflows name the checks that must pass before a change lands.

What this architecture does not claim

It does not claim a provider is available. Availability is the provider's, and the chain exists because it varies.

It does not claim a price is correct. It records the source that stated it and says when none did.

It does not claim a model can reason. It records the fields the host parses and sends only what both sides can express.

It does not claim the proxy is an authenticator. The subscription client gate reads an attribution field; it does not verify a claim.

Request path

Provider routing

Credential health

Cost provenance

## Cost provenance: where every number comes from
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/architecture/cost-provenance/

Where a price came from

A cost is only useful if you can tell how it was produced. MCC prices a request once, as it is logged, and stores the rung of the pricing ladder that answered each field beside the number. A figure no source states is shown as not priced, with the reason. That is what cost provenance means here: every number carries the source that stated it.

The ladder

Model metadata is resolved by a single ten-rung ladder, and cost is one of the fields it answers. The provider's own model list is the first rung; models.dev follows; the LiteLLM map is consulted when it is switched on; a cross-provider vote covers what remains; and a field no rung can answer is unpriced. The same resolver answers context, output limit, vision, tool support and the four cache prices, and the Models page and every generated agent catalogue read it, so they cannot disagree about a number or about where it came from.

The pricing ladder: each field walks its rungs, and the rung that answered is stored.

A diagram of five rungs: provider list, models.dev, LiteLLM when on, cross-provider vote, and unpriced.

A model's billed and estimated row: two figures kept apart, each with its own source.

When the provider's own list states a value, the badge reads provider or models.dev with no rung, because the enrichment step that merged them keeps no record of which won. When the ladder supplied it, the rung is exact, down to a cross-provider vote over strangers who merely share a name, which is badged approximate. Nothing about a request is reconstructed after the fact.

One price, one log row

A request is priced at the moment it is logged, and the rung that answered each price is stored in the row. That is what makes a total traceable: a number on a card can be followed back to the requests that produced it, and each request names its source. The attempt-level export writes one row per model the chain tried, so a fallback that spent tokens is in the export even though it did not answer.

Anthropic's split of cache writes into five-minute and one-hour writes is recorded, and a one-hour write is priced at a rate a source states, or shown as not priced with the reason. Requests that predate the split keep their five-minute price; a historical row is not repriced by a later release.

Reported, estimated, unpriced

Reported and estimated are two figures and are never summed. A reported figure is one a source stated; an estimated figure is one the install computed. Both are shown with their own priced-of-total denominator, so a partial figure cannot read as a complete one. A request no source could price is a dash, not a zero, and a request with no price does not quietly enter a total as if it cost nothing.

Reported, estimated and unpriced, with denominators that stop a partial figure reading as complete.

A diagram of three cost states, reported, estimated and unpriced, each with its own denominator and no summing.

The Cost panel: reported and estimated kept apart, each total carrying its priced-of-total denominator.

The all-time strip below the stat cards is never pruned, so it keeps counting after stored rows roll over at the retention cap. All time in a range control means all time still stored, and the two figures are labelled so they cannot be confused.

Usage is not cost

What a provider says is left is a different figure from what a request cost. The Usage page shows the Claude and ChatGPT subscription windows with their reset times, the credits and rate-limit figures that Nous Portal, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Kimi and Command Code send on responses you already get, and a Read now button that asks seven providers for their own figure. A window and a cash balance are two blocks and never one total. A provider that publishes a percentage is shown as a percentage, with no currency sign beside it.

The honesty note on a cost panel: an unpriceable request is a dash, and every total names its denominator.

A read can never charge a key or bench a provider. The page refreshes on its own only while it is open, at an interval you set, once per provider, and a hidden tab reads nothing. A 429 skips only the provider that sent it, and a repeatedly failing provider backs off on its own.

Media and the marketplace

Media requests are priced like chat ones: a provider figure, then models.dev, then LiteLLM when on, else unpriced. A Mistral image is recorded unpriced because no source publishes a per-image rate for it, and MCC never invents one. InferHub is a marketplace rather than an ordinary provider: a profile sets a price ceiling, and MCC sends that ceiling on every attempt so a request is never charged above it.

Limits and behaviour

A price is never invented, rounded up to a plausible number or copied from an old README.

A total with no denominator is not published.

A request whose cost came from an estimate is marked as estimated, not reported.

The all-time figure and the stored-window figure are separate and labelled.

A media model that a provider declares no price for stays unpriced.

Feature: analytics and cost with provenance

Data: where the priced row lives

Routing: which model the price belongs to

Glossary: rung, provenance, denominator

## Credential health and key rotation
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/architecture/credential-health/

How a key earns a bench

A provider holding several keys has to answer two independent questions about one failure: should another key be tried, and does this failure cost the credential anything? MCC answers each from its own allow-list, rather than from one deny-list that defaults to blaming the key. This page is the credential health internals: the two questions, the allow-list behind each, and the per-key attribution that follows.

Question one: try another key?

Only three failures justify a different credential: an auth rejection, a 429 and a transport fault. A different credential means a different account or a different connection, so one of them might help. Nothing else does. Every key in the pool reaches the same model and would meet the same timeout, 5xx, 410 or 400, so those raise out of the rotating loop and the fallback chain moves on to the next model instead.

Credentials already tried in a request are passed to the pool as an avoid set, so rotation cannot end with keys untried. The timeout class is excluded by name, because a model that never answered is not a broken socket and spending the whole pool on it would be a self-inflicted outage.

A key pool, the four rotation policies and the three failures that justify another key.

A diagram of a key pool with healthy, benched and locked-out keys, four rotation policies and the three failures that try another key.

Question two: what does it cost the credential?

Only the three signals that describe the credential charge it. A 401 or 403 walks an escalating lockout ladder: five minutes, one hour, one day by default, one step per consecutive rejection, staying at the last entry. A 429 is benched for exactly the wait the provider published, or for the configured cooldown when it published none, under the operator's ceiling. That bench is scoped to the (key, model) pair, and it leaves the slot healthy, because a gateway that limits one model has made no statement about the key's other models.

An exhausted-credit refusal is different. Where the provider says in words that the account behind the key has no balance left, the whole key is benched for the cooldown window, because a wallet is not per model. The matcher reads only the provider's own structured words, through an echo-safe reader, so a prompt that happens to contain a billing phrase cannot bench a key. A bare 402 that names no phrase rotates and falls through but charges nothing.

The three signals and what each one costs. Everything else leaves health untouched.

A diagram of three health signals: a rejected credential walks a lockout ladder, a 429 benches a key-and-model pair, and an exhausted balance benches the whole key.

The key itself is benched only once a configured number of distinct models hold a live bench on it at the same time, for the longest window already published and never less than the triggering 429 asked for. No ladder and no escalation beyond that one step are invented.

The credential-health card: the lockout ladder and the rate-limit cooldown, plus the per-pool rotation policy.

Rotate the pool, or route around the model?

Not every 429 should rotate. When route-around is on, the pool reports the failure, decides health as usual, and then raises a typed model-rate-limited signal. The executor moves to the next chain model on that same provider, because that is where the evidence points: on one measured request all three keys refused one model inside 0.2 seconds each while another model answered on the first key in the same second. With no such model on the chain, one bounded diagnostic probe on a model the operator already configured there decides whether to keep the scoped bench or promote it to the whole key.

The probe's clock belongs to the executor; the pool holds none of its own. That deliberate cost is that a key failing 5xx or transport on every request is retried once per request rather than benched, because the failure classes that could identify a dead key were the same ones emptying healthy pools.

One mechanism, two tunings

The rotation engine exists once, in core, and each frontend parameterises it. The provider tuning reaches neither the generic cooldown ladder nor the circuit breaker, because a provider adapter never classifies a failure as transient. The web-search tuning keeps both, because a search key that keeps erroring is worth resting. No half-open probe state remains: a slot reserved on acquire used to outlive a request that reported neither success nor failure, leaving the key unselectable until reset by hand, so a credential now wakes straight to healthy at the cost of at most one extra failed request.

Per-key attribution

Every request records which key answered, and the key is shown by name where a name exists and by a mask where it does not. The Analytics key filter still matches a renamed key's history by its mask, and the exports carry both the mask and the name. A masked label two keys share resolves to no name at all rather than to a guess.

Per-key performance: requests, error rate, cache hit and latency, with the errors each key actually returned.

Limits and behaviour

A country refusal is about the address, not the key: it never locks a key out on any route.

The pool never invents a ceiling: a wait comes from the provider's own headers or the configured window.

A key's health is decided before the response is committed and is visible in the request log afterwards.

Rotation changes which key is tried, never which model a route points at.

Feature: providers and credential health

Provider routing: the chain that follows a key's refusal

Observability: per-key attribution

Configuration: CREDENTIAL_* and RATE_LIMIT_*

## Data and storage: what MCC keeps and where
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/architecture/data-and-storage/

What is stored, and where

Everything MCC keeps is under one configurable directory on your machine. There is no remote database, no account and no second copy. What is stored is deliberately split between a settings file, a request log and a set of documents that a settings save must never rewrite. This page is the LLM gateway storage layout: what is written, where it lives, and what is never stored at all.

The configuration home

A new install keeps everything in ~/.mcc : the .env , the request log under logs/ , the per-agent documents the launchers write, and the JSON documents that do not belong in a settings file because they hold more than a scalar. MCC_CONFIG_DIR pins the directory to an absolute path and must be set in the shell, because the directory has to be known before there is a file to read.

The configuration home and the documents beside the .env.

A diagram of the configuration home with the .env, the request log, updates and cache, and the JSON documents beside them.

The split is deliberate. A custom provider's static credential travels on its descriptor rather than through a settings field, so it lives in custom_providers.json and a settings save cannot rewrite it. Learned facts live in their own document because they expire on a clock and are forgettable per row. Per-agent tier overrides live in their own document because a dashboard write must land without a restart, which it does by caching on the file's own timestamp.

The request log

The request log is a local SQLite database, logs/requests.db . A completed request is written once with its endpoint, harness, provider, key, model, status, turn, tokens, cost, time to first token and duration, plus the attempts it walked and the rung that priced it. A request answered by a local optimization records no provider, because none served it, and carries the rule and the tokens it saved for exactly those rows.

Columns cannot be added to an existing database by an open; the code that opens the log knows which columns its version requires and mirrors them in one place. That is why an older log keeps working rather than being silently migrated into an unusable shape.

The log, its search index, its chunk store and the analytics built over them.

A diagram of a completed request written to requests.db, with a search index, a prompt chunk store and analytics over the log.

The search index and the chunk store

Searching the log does not unpack every stored request. The search index stores each distinct piece of text in its own file beside the log. New requests are indexed as they are written; older ones are indexed when you press Build search index. The prompt chunk store keeps each repeated prompt part once, so turn N+1 of a conversation no longer stores turn N again. History is converted in the background, each prompt is read back byte for byte before it is replaced, and Pause and Continue sit beside the log's size.

Retention is a cap. REQUEST_LOG_MAX_ROWS prunes the oldest rows periodically, so the database does not grow without bound; once the cap is reached the log is a rolling window. The all-time strip on Analytics is kept separately and is never pruned, which is why a count can keep rising after the stored rows have rolled over.

Credentials and OAuth stores

OAuth credentials live in owner-only stores in the configuration home. MCC's own store is separate from Claude Code's, and MCC never refreshes Claude Code's file in place: rotating it would log out the real client, so a shared credential is renewed under Claude Code's own lock and written back by compare-and-swap. A credential read from another application's file is read-only to MCC unless it is explicitly MCC's own.

Logs and diagnostics

The server log rotates at 50 MB and retains five rotated files, bounding normal on-disk usage. API payloads and streamed events are not logged raw unless explicitly enabled. Values under keys that look like an API key, an authorization, a token or a secret are redacted where structured traces are emitted. Messaging text, transcription previews, CLI diagnostics and detailed messaging exception strings each have their own diagnostic flag, so a normal install does not record a conversation by accident.

The storage panel: the request log's size, its retention, and the controls that keep it bounded.

What is never stored remotely

There is no telemetry and no call home.

There is no remote request log and no account to reconcile against.

The only outbound traffic is a request to a provider you configured, a search service you enabled, or a web page a client asked to fetch.

A generated media file is stored only when storage is switched on, and with its own size cap.

One logged request: the attempts, tokens, timing and reasoning fields stored with it.

Limits and behaviour

A configuration save and a credential refresh write different files, so one cannot corrupt the other.

The log is local SQLite; a second MCC server with a different configuration home has its own log.

Retention prunes the oldest rows; the all-time figure survives it.

The search index returns the same results as a full scan.

A legacy configuration home is moved by one atomic rename, nothing copied or merged.

Configuration: the configuration home and the .env

Cost: what the stored price means

Feature: the request log and analytics

Platform: the legacy-home migration

## Provider routing and the fallback ladder
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/architecture/provider-routing/

From a tier name to one real model

The router answers one question: which concrete provider model serves this request, with which reasoning preference, and what happens if it cannot. It is deliberately small, and the rules it follows are the product's contract. This page is the provider routing internals: the three ways to name a model, the tier map, and the order the fallback ladder is walked in.

Three ways to name a model

Resolution takes three forms. A direct provider model ref names the provider and the exact model. A gateway model ID is decoded by the gateway-ID codec. The five tier aliases are intercepted ahead of both, and are pointers rather than models. If the incoming name is not direct, the router maps it by Claude tier: a name containing fable, opus, sonnet or haiku uses the matching tier override when set, and otherwise falls back to the default model.

The router also selects the reasoning preference. A direct ref uses the root policy; a Claude tier route uses a non-inherited tier override or the root fallback; the no-thinking gateway variant forces off. The application layer combines that preference with the concrete client request exactly once, and the resulting plan owns both the selected route and the final request-scoped policy.

The tier map, with a primary model and an ordered chain per route.

A diagram of five tiers, each with a primary model and fallback rows, one paused.

What the picker is told

The model-listing route advertises configured provider refs, cached provider-discovered models, no-thinking variants where appropriate, and built-in Claude model IDs for compatibility. A discovered model's thinking support is used for presentation only; it never selects request behaviour. A per-client picker is shaped outside the route: the composition bridge builds catalogue records from the same ladder, using the same visibility filter and projection, so a model cannot appear in one surface and not the other, and it writes each harness's catalogue without making a loopback HTTP request.

One consequence is worth stating because it is visible: a catalogue is a snapshot. The Codex App reads its catalogue at startup, so it must restart to see a later publication, and the Codex launcher remains a launch-time synchroniser for the same reason. An existing last-known-good catalogue is preserved when a projection resolves no routable models.

Aliases are pointers

The protocol names mcc/cyber , mcc/best , mcc/good , mcc/medium , mcc/cheap and mcc/vision serve harnesses that have no Claude vocabulary of their own. Each names one of the router's global routes, together with that route's fallback chain and pause list, and an unset route collapses onto the default model exactly as the Claude tier does. The provider ID mcc is reserved so a custom provider cannot make an alias ambiguous.

The tier segment is matched exactly, not by substring. The router takes an optional harness name from the request header or the user-agent fingerprint; an unidentified request resolves against the global chain rather than failing. The resolved tier route is recorded on the plan, which is what lets the request log name the tier, its source and its harness without adding a column to the log.

Walking the chain

Each route has a model and an ordered chain of stand-ins. The executor attempts the route's model first, then each entry in order. A model listed twice is tried twice, and each listing is judged when it is reached. A paused entry keeps its place and is never tried: no attempt is spent, no deadline is consumed, and the log records the reason.

A walked chain: skipped, answered and never reached, each with its reason.

A diagram of a four-model chain with a cooldown, a pause, an answer and an unreached model.

The chain's decision rules come from the failure, not from a general retry count. An auth rejection, a 429 and a transport fault can all be helped by a different key, so the pool rotates. A timeout, a 5xx, a 410 or a plain 400 cannot: every key talks to the same model and would hear the same answer, so those raise out of the rotating loop and the chain moves to the next model. A timeout is explicitly excluded from the transport-fault class, because a model that never answered is not a broken socket.

The chain as the request log shows it: each attempt with its key, timings and the reason it was or was not tried.

Media rails are not chat tiers

The image, speech, transcription and video rails walk their chains under the same rules through a separate copy of the engine, and a contract test holds the two copies to the same decisions. They keep their own key, model and proxy health, so a media failure never benches anything for chat. Nothing on a media rail is listed in the model catalogue or offered to a coding agent.

Limits and behaviour

The router never inspects an upstream model name or version to choose reasoning behaviour.

A route whose every model is paused fails with an error naming the key rather than silently falling through.

A failure after the first streamed chunk is not retried; the response is already committed.

An unknown harness is served, not refused.

A catalogue write that resolves no routable models preserves the last good file.

Feature: routing and fallback chains

Request path: where resolution sits

Credential health: what the chain asks the pool

Configuration: MODEL_* and the chain variables

## Request path: from a door to a committed reply
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/architecture/request-path/

From a door to a committed reply

A request is authenticated once, correlated once, routed once and executed against one provider at a time. The hard part is not the happy path; it is deciding when a failure is still an HTTP error and when it is already part of a stream. This page is the LLM request path, from the door the client entered by to the point the reply is committed.

The routes

The proxy exposes POST /v1/messages for Anthropic Messages, POST /v1/responses for OpenAI Responses, POST /v1/chat/completions for Chat Completions, POST /v1/messages/count_tokens for Anthropic token counting, GET /v1/models for the gateway and Claude-compatible model list, GET /health , POST /stop , and HEAD and OPTIONS probes on the supported endpoints. Google's surface lives in its own module because its path shape is unlike every other route: POST /v1beta/models/{model}:generateContent and its streaming, token-count and list siblings.

The four client protocols and the routes they enter.

A diagram showing four client protocols entering four routes that meet one router.

Authentication and correlation

Proxy authentication is one function. If ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN is blank, proxy authentication is disabled. Otherwise the proxy accepts exactly a bearer token, and other credential headers are ignored, so a stale provider key cannot mask valid proxy authorization. The complete token is compared in constant time, and no model suffix or other token mutation is accepted.

A pure ASGI boundary creates one opaque request ID before routing, places it in the log context and request state, and adds it to the response while forwarding the real response-start message. The Responses surface and the shared model catalogue expose the same value as a request-id header. Provider execution receives that existing ID; it never creates a second one. Keeping the context around the whole inner call is what preserves correlation during streaming.

Routing and shaping

The product handler validates the request, resolves the model and the reasoning intent, applies Claude-only safety-classifier and local-optimization policy, handles local server tools, and then asks the executor to stream the routed request. The Responses handler is streaming-only and delegates its protocol work to an adapter that converts the payload into an Anthropic Messages request before execution and converts the streamed events back afterwards.

Seven stages from ingress to a priced, logged reply.

A numbered seven-stage pipeline: ingress, route, shape, credential, attempt, fallback and reply, ending in one price and log row.

The result of the pipeline: one request's attempts, with a reason beside every model it did not try.

The commit boundary

The executor resolves a provider from the current generation, synchronously preflights the upstream request, emits trace events, counts input tokens and returns an iterator of protocol events. The response layer then waits for the first protocol chunk before it returns a successful streaming response. That wait is the commit boundary. A provider failure before it stays a typed non-2xx JSON response, and that response carries a retry header set to false, because MCC retains ownership of upstream retry rather than causing a second client retry loop.

After the first chunk has escaped, HTTP status is committed. The Messages surface then emits an Anthropic error event and closes without a synthetic message-stop; the Responses surface emits a failed response with its original ID. Non-streaming Messages requests aggregate internally and return a non-2xx JSON for any terminal stream error, discarding incomplete content rather than presenting a partial success.

Close ownership

The public response chain follows a transitive close-ownership rule. A response owns its replay iterator; replay owns the active protocol adapter; each adapter owns its direct input; tracing owns the executor body; the executor body owns the provider iterator; and the provider runner owns its upstream stream. Each owner closes its direct input on normal completion, failure, cancellation and early consumer close. A generation lease is released only after the body chain has finished closing.

Failures that are not provider failures

Ingress authentication, request validation, model routing and deterministic preflight failures are ordinary HTTP errors and do not receive the terminal retry header. Missing provider configuration and a shutting-down request runtime are application-readiness errors: the Messages surface serialises them as Anthropic JSON and the Responses surface as OpenAI JSON, and neither is misclassified as an already-finalised provider failure.

The Gemini difference

The Gemini door keeps Google's error envelope, because Gemini CLI branches on the status string when it decides whether to retry. Its prompt token count includes the cached prompt, unlike Anthropic's, because Google's field includes it and reports the served part separately; a straight rename would under-report every cached request. Its stream has no done sentinel, because that is OpenAI's convention and Google's client would try to parse it as JSON.

A request detail: what entered, what was routed, what was sent and what answered.

Limits and behaviour

One request ID, created at ingress, is reused by every stage. There is no second identifier.

A failure after the first chunk cannot change the HTTP status; it is an in-band event.

A non-streaming request discards an incomplete reply rather than returning partial content as success.

The executor depends on a provider port, not on a provider implementation, which is why four doors can share one executor.

Provider routing: what happens inside the routed stage

Credential health: what happens before an attempt

Feature: routing and fallback chains

Glossary: commit boundary, generation lease, request ID

## Security model: keys, boundaries and local-first
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/architecture/security-model/

The principles the boundary is built on

This page states what MCC does to keep a local proxy local, and what it refuses to do. It is a description of the design, not a security audit, and it makes no claim that a deployment is safe without the operator's own choices. It is the LLM gateway security model: local by default, a token once it leaves the machine, owner-only stores, redacted logs and narrow egress.

The threat model starts from one fact: the proxy holds the keys to providers that bill. A local service with those keys has to be reachable by the tools that need it and by nothing else. The principles below are how the code enforces that, and each one has a visible consequence.

Five principles: local by default, a token once it leaves, owner-only stores, redacted logs and narrow egress.

A diagram listing five security principles with a one-line consequence for each.

Local by default

The admin UI and the admin APIs are loopback-only. They have no login because they are not reachable from another machine, and the proxy's own listen address is a setting the operator chooses. The dashboard does not open a second port and does not embed a remote widget.

A token once it leaves this machine

Proxy authentication is a bearer token. When it is set, the proxy accepts exactly that token, compares it in constant time, and ignores other credential headers so a stale provider key cannot mask valid proxy authorization. When the host is opened to other machines and the token is empty, the server refuses to start rather than serving an unauthenticated proxy. The token is generated for the machine on first start and lives in the configuration home.

Owner-only stores

OAuth credentials live in owner-only files, and a login a proxy listener asks for is stored owner-only and never shown again. A credential read from another application's file is read-only to MCC. The configuration home is one directory, so an operator can see and protect everything in one place rather than hunting for scattered state.

The boundary: local surfaces, the token guard and the single outbound path.

A diagram of the local dashboard and proxy, the token guard and the only outbound path to configured providers.

Redacted by default

Values under keys that look like an API key, an authorization, a token or a secret are redacted where structured traces are emitted. API payloads and streamed events are not logged raw unless explicitly enabled. The provider's own bytes are kept only behind an opt-in flag. Messaging text, transcription previews and CLI diagnostics each have their own flag, so a normal install does not record a conversation by accident.

Narrow egress

The only outbound traffic is a request to a provider the operator configured, a search service the operator enabled, or a web page a client asked to fetch. There is no telemetry and no call home. Web fetch enforces its allowed URL schemes and blocks private-network targets unless the operator explicitly allows them. Local provider status checks are exposed only through the local admin API.

Evidence over assertion

A price is recorded with the source that stated it. A skipped model is a row with its reason. A key's health is decided from the provider's own signals, and a bench duration is never invented. The same discipline is applied to this site: every claim is recorded against a path or a command in the repository, and a figure that cannot be traced is not published.

What this page does not claim

It does not claim the software is free of defects. No such claim is made anywhere on this site.

It does not claim a deployment is safe regardless of how it is configured. Opening the proxy without a token is refused, but the operator still chooses the address, the network and the keys.

It does not describe an audit, a penetration test or a certification, and none is implied.

It does not repeat a known issue as a public roadmap. Issues are handled in the repository's own channel.

Credential health is one of the visible controls: a key is judged only on the provider's own signals.

Operating principles for the reader

Keep the proxy on loopback unless a client on another machine genuinely needs it; if it needs it, set the token and put the proxy behind a network you control.

Use a separate key per machine or per purpose, so a key can be revoked without taking everything down.

Read a provider's own terms before routing a subscription credential through any proxy. MCC documents the Anthropic subscription position rather than hiding it.

Treat the configuration home as a secret. It holds the keys, the stores and the log.

Prefer a short retention window and raw logging off unless you are actively diagnosing a request.

Data and storage: what the configuration home holds

Credential health: the provider's own signals

Licence: AGPL-3.0-or-later or commercial

Configuration: HOST, PORT and the token variable

## Configuration: how MCC settings are provided
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/configuration/

How settings are provided

MCC has one configuration home, one .env and one set of documents beside it. The dashboard writes the file, the server reads it, and the launchers resolve the same directory. There is no second configuration system to reconcile. This page is the LLM gateway configuration map: the home, the file, the documents beside it and the variables that are read before the file is.

The configuration home

A new install keeps everything in ~/.mcc . That directory holds the .env , the request log under logs/ , the per-agent documents the launchers write, and the JSON documents that do not belong in a settings file: custom provider definitions, per-agent tier overrides, credential names, OAuth stores, model overrides, learned facts, proxy chains and marketplace profiles. An install from before 6.40.0 is migrated from its legacy directory on its first start by one atomic rename, nothing copied or merged, and the startup log always names the directory in use.

One variable resolves before the file does. MCC_CONFIG_DIR pins the configuration home to an absolute path and overrides every default. It must be set in your shell, not written into the .env, because the directory has to be known before there is a file to read. Set it for the mcc-* launchers too, or they will read a different directory than the server.

The .env

The .env is the settings file. Every setting lives there with the same name it has in the documentation, and the dashboard writes the same file, so a value set on a page and a value set by hand are the same value. On a new install the server writes the file on first start and generates the proxy token for that machine.

The repository ships an annotated example file, .env.example , with inline comments and cost notes. Its variable names are public; its values are not, and this site never publishes one. For a secret-like setting the configuration page on this site gives the name and the purpose only.

The documents beside the .env

Document

What it holds

custom_providers.json

custom provider definitions, including their static credentials

harness_tiers.json

per-agent tier overrides

credential_names.json

display names for keys, keyed by a hash of the key

model_overrides.json

operator overrides for a model's fields

learned_facts.json

what this install learned about a provider, with expiry

proxy_chains.json

named proxy chains and their exits

marketplace_profiles.json

InferHub price-ceiling profiles

anthropic_oauth.json

MCC's own OAuth credential store, owner-only

chatgpt-oauth.json

the ChatGPT OAuth store

logs/requests.db

the request log

Environment variables that are not settings

A settings save and a credential refresh write different files. That split is what lets a provider be re-keyed without rewriting the routing map, and a tier change without touching an OAuth store. It is also why the dashboard can show a key round-trip and a tier change as two independent actions rather than one save that rewrites everything.

A few variables are read before or outside the settings file. MCC_CONFIG_DIR chooses the directory. MCC_ENV_FILE names an explicit dotenv file to load instead of the default one. The install scripts read MCC_INSTALL_NO_START and MCC_INSTALL_NO_DESKTOP , and the npm wrapper reads MCC_NPM_INSTALL . HTTPS_PROXY , HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY are honoured by the installers and by outbound requests.

Editing rules

A blank value means unset. Removing a value from the page writes a blank, and the default applies.

A restart-required setting is labelled on the page; Apply does not pretend it took effect.

A managed write backs the file up before it changes it.

A leftover setting from a removed feature is ignored at startup and dropped on the next save.

The launchers read the same directory as the server; a mismatch is the one configuration mistake the product cannot fix for you.

Environment reference: the variable names, grouped by area

The dashboard: where most settings are edited

Architecture: what is stored and where

Quick start: the first settings you will touch

## Frequently asked questions about the gateway
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/faq/

Questions this site is asked most

Each answer below is written from the product's own documentation and, where it matters, from the source. The same questions and answers are published as structured data for search engines, generated from this one list so the two cannot drift. It is the LLM gateway FAQ: the questions this site is asked most, answered once.

What is My Claude Code?

A local multi-provider LLM proxy, model router and control plane for AI coding agents. You point the agents at one address on your machine and manage providers, keys, routing, reasoning, budgets, web search and cost in one place.

Does it send anything to a remote server?

No. It has no telemetry and phones home to nothing. Its only outbound traffic goes to the providers you configure, a search service you enable, or a web page a client asked to fetch. The dashboard and admin APIs are loopback-only.

Which coding agents can use it?

Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and OpenCode 2, Gemini CLI, Crush, Cline, Goose, Aider, Kimi Code, Qwen Code, Command Code, OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Droid, Pi and Kilo have launchers. Desktop apps and other clients are configured from the dashboard or pointed at the proxy directly.

Which providers are supported?

Sixty provider cards across cloud APIs, subscription and OAuth sign-ins, gateways, local servers and marketplaces, from Anthropic and OpenAI to OpenRouter, Mistral, Gemini, Vertex, DeepSeek, Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp. Local models connect through a base URL rather than a key, and any other OpenAI-compatible endpoint can be added as a custom provider.

Is it free?

MCC itself is free under AGPL-3.0-or-later, or a commercial licence by negotiation. The models behind it may be free, paid, subscription-based or local; that is your choice and your account.

Does it work without an API key?

Yes, for the free path. A fresh install routes the Mythos, Fable, Opus and Sonnet tiers to OpenCode Zen's free model with no key at all. The default model and the Haiku tier still point at NVIDIA NIM, so they need a key or a new model.

Where do my keys live?

In one configuration home on your machine, by default ~/.mcc . The .env holds the settings, and the documents beside it hold custom providers, OAuth stores and credential names. MCC never sends a key anywhere except the provider it belongs to.

What happens when a provider is down?

The fallback chain walks to the next model. A model that errors, rate-limits or refuses moves the request down its chain, and the first attempt that succeeds ends the walk. Every step is recorded in the request log with its reason.

Does it retry the same model forever?

No. A 429 benches the key and model pair for the wait the provider published, and the chain moves on. A timeout, a 5xx, a 410 or a plain 400 is treated as the model's answer, so the chain tries a different model instead of spending the rest of the key pool.

Can I use a Claude subscription?

MCC can route an Anthropic subscription credential, but Anthropic's published terms do not permit routing Free, Pro or Max plan credentials on behalf of third-party users, and the risk is to your account. MCC documents the position in full rather than hiding it; read the Anthropic subscription page before enabling it.

What is a tier?

A coding-agent route such as Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku or Mythos, mapped to a real model and an ordered chain. Tier aliases such as mcc/cyber and mcc/best are protocol names for those routes, not models.

What is a fallback chain?

An ordered list of stand-ins behind a route. If the model a request routes to cannot serve it, the next entry is tried, then the next. A model listed twice is tried twice. A paused entry keeps its place and is never tried.

What does a 429 do to my key?

It benches that key for that one model, for exactly the wait the provider published or a configured cooldown when it published none. The key stays healthy for its other models. The key itself is benched only once several models hold a live bench at once.

Can I use several keys per provider?

Yes. Put them in one comma-separated variable and choose a policy: single, round robin, least used or failover. Each key gets its own upstream client and rate-limit window, and the order in the pool is the order the policy reads.

How is cost calculated?

Each request is priced once, as it is logged. The price comes from a ladder: the provider's own model list first, then models.dev, then LiteLLM when it is switched on, then a cross-provider vote. The source that answered is stored beside the number.

Why are reported and estimated cost separate?

Because they are different claims. A reported figure is one a source stated; an estimated figure is one the install computed. MCC never sums them, and every total carries a priced-of-total denominator so a partial figure cannot read as a complete one.

Does it log my prompts?

The request log stores completed requests locally and is searchable across prompt, reply, reasoning and tool calls. It is on by default and controlled by REQUEST_LOG_ENABLED , with a row cap that prunes the oldest rows. Raw provider bytes and payloads are separate opt-in flags. The log is local SQLite, and a hidden dashboard tab reads nothing.

Can I search my request log?

Yes. The search index stores each distinct piece of text in its own file beside the log, so a search does not unpack every stored request. New requests are indexed as they are written, and older ones when you press Build search index.

How do I connect Claude Code?

Run mcc-claude . For the native model picker, run mcc-claude --discover-models . The dashboard's Configure Claude Code page can also write MCC's proxy settings into Claude Code's own settings file.

How do I connect Codex?

Run mcc-codex . It speaks the OpenAI Responses surface and keeps its own generated catalogue, because the Codex App reads that catalogue at startup and must restart to see a later one.

Can I use a local model?

Yes. LM Studio, llama.cpp and Ollama are provider cards that need a base URL rather than a key, and they sit behind the same address and the same routing as a cloud provider.

Does it support images?

Yes. A vision adapter can divert an image request to a model that can see, and describe mode has a sighted model describe each image for a blind tier. Outbound pictures are resized to a 1568-pixel long edge on the router's own copy.

Does it do web search?

Yes. Claude Code's web_search and web_fetch tools are fulfilled at the proxy instead of by Anthropic, over fifteen search backends or a keyless fallback. No Anthropic search credits are used.

Can I run it from Discord or Telegram?

Yes, optionally. A messaging bridge turns chat messages into managed coding-agent sessions, with voice-note transcription and stop and clear commands. It is off by default and skipped cleanly when it is not configured.

What platforms does it run on?

Windows, macOS and Linux, as a server or as a native desktop app with a tray. The one-liners install a managed Python 3.14 through uv, so no system Python is needed. The desktop app is a window onto the same server.

How do I update it?

The dashboard announces releases and installs them with checksum verification, or re-run the install command, which always fetches the newest release. An update is atomic: the new version is built beside the running one and swapped in only after it answers the health check. The desktop window shows each stage while it runs.

How do I uninstall it?

Run the uninstall one-liner, or mcc uninstall if you installed through npm. It verifies every MCC command is gone before it reports success. The desktop app is removed separately, through the platform's own mechanism.

Is it affiliated with Anthropic, OpenAI or Google?

No. My Claude Code is an independent open-source project. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or OpenCode. Claude, Codex, ChatGPT and Gemini are trademarks of their owners. Provider names are used to describe what the software connects to, not to claim a relationship.

Where is the full documentation?

The repository's docs/ directory holds the complete usage guide, the routing reference, the architecture file and the per-surface guides. The dashboard's Docs page renders the same documents offline for the version you installed.

Why does the dashboard not open?

The usual reasons are a server that is not running, a different port, or a configuration directory the launcher and the server do not share. Check mcc-server --version , then the health endpoint, then MCC_CONFIG_DIR if you set it.

Still stuck?

The troubleshooting page covers the failures this site can verify, with the symptom, the cause and the fix. For anything else, the repository's issue tracker is the channel, and a security report has its own private route.

Troubleshooting: verified symptoms and fixes

Quick start: install and the first five minutes

Features: every capability in depth

Licence: the exact terms

## Features: every capability of the local LLM gateway
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/features/

Every capability, with a deep page for each

MCC is deep because a proxy that sits in front of every coding agent has to be. Each area below has its own page, written from the source and the product's own documentation, with real screenshots of the dashboard where the feature lives. This page is the index of LLM gateway features: every capability area, with a deep page for each.

The shortcut below is the whole product in one sentence: one address, every provider you configure, and a control plane that keeps the model, the credential, the reasoning setting and the cost in one place. The pages after it go one area at a time.

The pages are written this way because the product is not one feature. A proxy that sits in front of sixteen agents and sixty providers has to answer the same question differently for each of them, and a one-page summary would either flatten that or repeat it. Each page takes one area and follows it through the code, the dashboard and the request log.

The order is deliberate: a reader who wants the architecture can start there, and a reader who wants to install can stop after the quick start. Nothing on a page depends on having read another first, though the related links at the foot of each one point at the neighbour that explains a term in more depth.

The Providers page: one searchable card per provider, each naming the setting that holds its key.

Model tiers and fallback chains

Tier aliases, per-agent overrides, ordered fallbacks, pausing, the vision adapter and describe mode.

Reasoning and budgets

One effort setting, adaptive reasoning, encrypted reasoning replay, prompt-cache lifetime, output ceilings and deadlines.

Providers and credentials

60 provider cards, custom providers, four rotation policies, key health, proxy chains and OAuth sign-ins.

Agent support

Launchers, dashboard installs, desktop-app Configure and Undo, generated catalogues and per-agent attribution.

Analytics and cost

The request log, search, rollups, latency, exports and cost with provenance.

Web search and fetch

The native server-tool proxy, 15 search backends, a keyless fallback and web fetch extraction.

Messaging

Discord and Telegram sessions, voice-note transcription, and the stop and clear commands.

Media routing

Image, edit, speech, transcription, translation and video endpoints over their own rails.

Platform and packaging

Windows, macOS and Linux, the desktop app and tray, the update path, npm and PyPI.

The CLI

The launchers, headless app control, the installer's flags and the migration command.

The dashboard

Every setting, local-only, with appearance, updates and the in-app docs.

How to read these pages

Each deep page answers the same questions in order: what the capability is, why it matters, how to use it with verified steps, what you see in the dashboard, and what its limits are. Configuration is named by variable, never by value. Where a feature depends on another, the related links at the foot of the page point at it.

A capability is on this site only when the code or the tests prove it exists. Every number is either computed from the repository or recorded against the command that produced it. If a page is not here, the feature did not meet that bar.

## Agent support: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/features/agents/

A first-class client for every agent

Claude Code is one client here, not the frame around everything else. MCC can launch the CLI agents, configure the desktop apps it cannot launch, generate a real model catalogue for each one, and name the agent behind every request in the log. The launchers are how a Claude Code agent, a Codex agent, an OpenCode agent and the rest are pointed at one address.

Every agent MCC can launch is declared in one registry, and the Coding agents page shows each one's installed state, its commands and flags with a copy button, its protocol and its generated catalogue. Applications MCC does not launch get a Configure button on the same page instead, which edits the one file each of them reads.

The Coding agents page: one card per agent, each with an Install or Configure button, its protocol and its catalogue.

The launchers

A launcher is a small command that points an agent at the local proxy and starts it. The set covers Claude Code ( mcc-claude ), Codex ( mcc-codex ), OpenCode and OpenCode 2 ( mcc-opencode , mcc-opencode2 ), Gemini CLI ( mcc-gemini ), Crush, Cline, Goose, Aider, Kimi Code, Qwen Code, Command Code, OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Droid, Pi and Kilo. mcc-claude --discover-models wires Claude Code's native /model picker to MCC's catalogue; mcc-claude-old keeps the older launch shape.

The launchers list: every mcc-* command MCC puts on your PATH, with its install state.

Claude Code's native model picker, listing the routed models through MCC's catalogue.

Installing an agent from the dashboard

An agent that is not installed gets an Install button on its card, with the vendor's own line beside it to copy instead. The plan is shown before anything runs: every download, command, permission prompt and PATH or profile change. The vendor's own installer is used first, npm only where it is the only way, and Node.js is installed first only when it is missing. MCC never runs sudo and never upgrades your Node.js.

Desktop apps: Configure and Undo

For an app MCC cannot launch, Configure writes MCC's keys into the one file that app reads and carries every other byte through. A .mcc-backup is taken before the first edit, a diff preview is shown before every write, and a drift badge appears after a hand-edit. Undo works two ways: remove only MCC's keys, or restore the exact values MCC replaced. The files MCC does not reformat are left alone.

Desktop apps: cards for the apps MCC does not launch, each with Configure, a backup note and an Undo path.

Claude Code's settings, edited from the dashboard: every setting the CLI reads, with a backup taken before the write.

The same work is available without a browser. mcc-apps list , mcc-apps status , mcc-apps configure [--preview] and mcc-apps undo [--restore] do what the buttons do, which matters on a headless machine.

Claude Desktop's connection dialog: a base URL and a gateway key field, the one place that app is pointed at MCC.

Generated catalogues

Each agent's model list is generated from the same metadata the router uses: real context windows, output ceilings, vision support, tool support and the host's own effort vocabulary. The composition bridge that writes a catalogue uses the same visibility filter, ref enumeration and projection as /v1/models , so a model cannot appear in one and not the other. Writes are atomic, identical bytes are not rewritten, and a last-known-good catalogue is preserved when a projection resolves no routable models.

Request attribution

Analytics names the coding agent behind every request. The harness is identified from the x-mcc-harness header or the request's user-agent fingerprint, and it drives both the log's attribution and the per-agent tier map. An unidentified request is not failed; it resolves against the global chain and is logged as unidentified.

The same attribution is what lets one agent run a different tier map from another without a second proxy. Claude Code can route Opus-tier traffic to one model and Codex to another while both talk to the same address.

Media tools for an agent

MCC's media server, mcc-mcp , gives an agent one tool per filled media rail, plus a free status tool. It is added per agent with an Add MCP server button and taken out with Remove. The buttons write only MCC's own launch lines and configuration layers, never your files; the token stays in MCC's settings; each agent's own prompt asks before a paid tool. It is off for every agent by default.

Other clients

Anything that speaks OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini can be pointed at the proxy, including VS Code's Copilot custom endpoint and the JetBrains ACP surface. The clients documentation carries an API reference with one runnable example per endpoint. An agent MCC cannot launch and an app MCC cannot configure are both still clients if the user points them here. A client that speaks one of the four protocols needs no plugin, and a client that speaks none of them is out of scope rather than half-supported.

A live Claude Code session running through the proxy, mid-conversation.

Limits and behaviour

A launcher whose agent is missing prints that agent's own install command and exits; it does not try to install the agent itself.

A drift badge appears when a hand-edit moves a configured file away from what MCC wrote.

A tool-returned image and a media request share the same rails and the same cost accounting as chat.

The Media server is off for every agent until it is added, and no agent button writes to a file MCC did not create.

Quick start: install and launch your first agent

Providers: what the agent is routed to

Observability: where the attribution appears

The CLI: the launchers and headless controls

Claude Code through the proxy: the mcc-claude command

Codex CLI through the proxy: the mcc-codex command

OpenCode through the proxy: the mcc-opencode command

Gemini CLI through the proxy: the mcc-gemini command

## The MCC command line
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/features/cli/

The commands MCC puts on your PATH

The dashboard is optional. Everything the page can do has a command, and the launchers are how most people start an agent. This page is the reference for the commands, with the flags that exist and the ones that do not. It is the reference for the LLM gateway CLI: mcc-server, the launchers and the headless tools beside them.

An install puts mcc-server and the mcc-* launchers on your PATH, and adds the headless tools beside them. A launcher whose agent is missing prints that agent's own install command and exits; it does not try to install the agent itself.

The launcher set is generated from one registry, so a new agent is a registry entry rather than a new script. A launcher whose agent is missing prints that agent's own install command and exits, which is why the CLI never installs an agent on its own.

The server and the launchers

Start the server

mcc-server

mcc-server --version prints the running release. The server listens on loopback port 8082 by default, serves the dashboard at /admin and answers /health . Every other MCC server on the machine is left alone.

Command

What it does

mcc-claude

launch Claude Code against the proxy; --discover-models wires the native model picker, and mcc-claude-old keeps the older launch shape

mcc-codex

launch Codex CLI over the OpenAI Responses surface

mcc-opencode , mcc-opencode2

launch OpenCode over Anthropic Messages

mcc-gemini

launch Gemini CLI over the Gemini API surface

mcc-crush , mcc-cline , mcc-goose , mcc-aider

launch the matching agent

mcc-kimi , mcc-qwen , mcc-commandcode

launch Kimi Code, Qwen Code and Command Code

mcc-openclaw , mcc-hermes , mcc-droid , mcc-pi , mcc-kilo

launch the matching agent

Claude Code's native model picker after mcc-claude --discover-models, listing the routed models.

Headless app control

mcc-apps does what the Desktop apps cards do, which matters on a headless machine or over SSH. Its subcommands are list , status , configure (with --preview to show the change without writing it) and undo (with --restore to put back the exact values MCC replaced).

Preview a desktop-app change

mcc-apps configure --preview

Sign-in, migration and the token optimizer

mcc-anthropic-oauth-login signs in from a terminal. It takes --paste , --no-browser , --list and --remove <id> , and answers --help without starting anything.

mcc-migrate runs the legacy-home move by hand. It refuses while it can see a live server.

mcc-rtk status|enable|disable|uninstall|apply controls the opt-in token optimizer per agent, the same control the dashboard's Token optimizer card writes.

mcc-desktop fetches and verifies the desktop app, and refuses rather than pretending on a machine with no tray.

A launcher starts the agent with the proxy address, the token and the catalogue in place; the agent itself looks unchanged.

The installer's flags

The one-liners accept --dry-run to see the plan without changing anything, --version to pin a release, --desktop to install the app too, --no-restart to leave a running server alone, --no-start to stop and start nothing, --no-desktop to leave the app alone and --yes-sudo to answer the sudo prompt for the Linux package step. The npm wrapper accepts --server-only , --desktop-only , --no-desktop and --yes-sudo , and reads MCC_NPM_INSTALL=server|desktop|both|none .

See what an install would do

curl -fsSL "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FiredMosquito831/my-claude-code/main/scripts/install.sh" | sh -s -- --dry-run

The dashboard lists every launcher it installed, with its state and a copy button.

A first run, in order

Install with the one-liner for your platform, then reopen the terminal so the PATH change is visible.

Run mcc-server ; on first start it writes the configuration home and generates the proxy token.

Add one provider key on the Providers page, then set the tiers on Model Config.

Launch the agent with its own command, for example mcc-claude . The launcher passes the proxy address, the token and the generated catalogue, and the agent itself looks unchanged.

Where the CLI and the dashboard meet

The command line and the dashboard are two front doors to one configuration. A command does not keep a private copy of a setting, and a page does not write somewhere the server will not read. mcc-apps configure shows the same diff preview the card shows, and mcc-apps undo performs the same two undo modes.

The exceptions are the things that must be decided before the settings file exists. MCC_CONFIG_DIR is a shell variable, not a setting, and the install-time switches are flags rather than values. Everything else has one name and one place, which is what makes a command and a page safe to use interchangeably.

A command that needs a provider key reads it from the same configuration home the server reads, through the same settings resolution. There is no separate credential path for the CLI, and no command that writes a key the dashboard would not show.

What the commands do not do

A launcher does not install its agent. It prints the agent's own install line and exits.

The installer does not install curl, and it does not upgrade your system Python. It uses Python 3.14 through uv.

The CLI does not write a file the dashboard does not also write; both go through the same configuration.

No command changes repository settings, DNS or a hosting account.

Quick start: the exact install commands

Agents: what each launcher starts

Platform: the desktop app and the update path

Configuration: how settings reach the commands

## The local control-plane dashboard
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/features/dashboard/

The local control panel

The Admin UI is local-only and is where everything is configured. It opens on a Get Started checklist and gets out of the way once dismissed. It reads and writes the same .env the server reads, so the page and the file never disagree. It is the LLM dashboard: the local control panel, and the one place every setting can be changed.

The dashboard is served by the server it configures, on loopback, at http://127.0.0.1:8082/admin . It has no login because it is not reachable from another machine. A change is collected on the page and written only when you press Apply, at the foot of the page, which validates first.

Get Started: the first-run checklist, from a provider key to a running agent.

The pages

Page

What it is for

Get Started

the first-run checklist: provider, tiers, an agent, optionally web search and analytics

Providers

one searchable card per provider: keys, key pools, rotation, per-key health and Refresh models

Configure Claude Code

pointing Claude Code at the proxy, per session or permanently

Coding agents

each launcher's installed state and flags, Install, and Configure and Undo for desktop apps

Model Config

the tier map, fallback chains, the vision adapter, reasoning control and the media rails

Models

every model every provider publishes, with bulk visibility, capability probes and learned facts

Web Search

route policy, the search chain, provider cards, key health and search analytics

Limits & Resilience

output budgets, deadlines and their calculator, chain benching, retries, credential health, diagnostics

Analytics

the request log and everything computed from it, plus storage settings

Token Optimizer

what never reached a provider, and the opt-in trimming and RTK controls

Messaging

the Discord or Telegram bot, its allowed scope and voice settings

Usage

what each provider says is left, in five layouts over one payload

Proxying

proxy chains, the local scan, Tor, VPN accounts and WireGuard runners

InferHub

the marketplace page: profile, balance read-only, offers and the market snapshot

Guide and Docs
