the task-oriented guide, and these documents rendered in the app

The Providers page in a fresh state, with its search box and the provider grid below.

Appearance

A page is a view over configuration, not a separate store. The Analytics page reads the request log; Model Config reads and writes the tier variables; the Providers page reads the key pools and the credential stores. Closing the browser changes nothing, and reopening it shows the server's current state rather than a cached copy.

The dashboard's own look is a feature. There are two designs, Today and Hybrid, the latter with a masthead, a numbered rail and a right-hand drawer; seven colour families, each in light and dark; and three densities. They are chosen per browser on Get Started, or machine-wide with ADMIN_DESIGN , ADMIN_THEME , ADMIN_MODE and ADMIN_DENSITY . A browser choice always wins, and a shell that cannot start falls back to Today with a one-line note.

Validate and Apply

The footer of a settings page validates before it writes. A setting the server can only read at startup is marked restart-required, so Apply cannot report success while a running server keeps using the old value. A managed write backs the file up first. The dashboard and the file are one source of truth: a value set by hand is shown on the page, and a value set on the page is in the file.

Updates

The sidebar shows the running version and live status. A newer release is announced with its changelog, and the Update button runs the same installer path as the command line: checksum verified, built beside the running version, run once, swapped in, and the previous version restored if the health check never answers.

The update banner: a newer release, its changelog and a one-click update that uses the same verified path as the CLI.

The version panel in the sidebar: the running release and a live status dot.

Local only, by construction

The admin UI and admin APIs are loopback-only.

The dashboard has no third-party analytics, no remote fonts and no embedded widgets.

A hidden tab reads nothing; the Usage page refreshes only while it is open.

The Docs page renders the documentation bundled with the installed version, so it works offline.

The page loads no remote font, script or image; its stylesheet and its one small script are served by the server itself.

Configuration

Most settings are written to the managed .env . The appearance settings are ADMIN_DESIGN , ADMIN_THEME , ADMIN_MODE and ADMIN_DENSITY ; the log retention settings are on the Analytics page; and the usage auto-refresh interval is USAGE_AUTO_REFRESH_SECONDS . The configuration home itself is MCC_CONFIG_DIR , which is environment-only and cannot be set from the dashboard.

Limits and behaviour

A restart-required change is labelled, not silently deferred.

A setting the page cannot validate is not written.

The dashboard never opens a port beyond the server's own address.

A browser-level appearance choice overrides a machine-wide one without changing it.

Observability: the Analytics page in depth

Web search: the Web Search page in depth

Configuration: how settings are provided

Gallery: every reviewed dashboard screen

## Media handling in the local LLM gateway
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/features/media/

Image, speech and video over the same engine

Media is not bolted on. The image, speech, transcription and video endpoints run over their own rails, but they share the chat engine's retry, key rotation, 429 handling and proxy rules, with health records of their own so a media failure never benches a model for chat. This page is the LLM media path: four rails, one engine, and the same logging and cost accounting as text.

A media request names a model on a media rail. MCC walks that rail's chain exactly as it walks a chat chain: the same deadlines, pauses, skip kinds and retry rules, through a separate copy of the engine that a contract test holds to chat's decisions. The rails keep their own key, model and proxy health, so a failed image request does not bench anything for a chat.

Endpoint

Rail

Settings

POST /v1/images/generations

Image

MODEL_IMAGE , MODEL_IMAGE_FALLBACKS , MODEL_IMAGE_PAUSED

POST /v1/images/edits

Image

the same rail

POST /v1/audio/speech

Speech

MODEL_TTS and its chain

POST /v1/audio/transcriptions , /v1/audio/translations

Transcription

MODEL_ASR and its chain

POST /v1/videos and the job endpoints

Video

MODEL_VIDEO and its chain

Gemini :generateContent with image or audio output, :predictLongRunning

Image, Speech, Video

the same rails

The image rail on Model Config: the media endpoints it serves and the label each row carries.

A provider serves only what it declares

A provider serves a media operation only when it declares that endpoint. MCC never guesses from a model name. A model on a provider that declares nothing for the operation is skipped and not charged a failure; the request log shows it as unsupported . An edit therefore skips every model whose provider declares no edit endpoint, uncharged, and is served by the first one that does.

Most image providers are passed through field for field: the body the client sent is forwarded with the model replaced by the rail's model, so a parameter only one host understands still reaches it, and the host's answer is returned as it came. Gemini's native speech and transcription surfaces and Mistral's image surface are translated instead. MCC builds those requests itself, lists any field it has no place for under not_forwarded on the request row rather than guessing, and turns the host's answer back into what an OpenAI client reads.

Mistral images are the unusual wire: Mistral does not document an image-generation endpoint. MCC asks for the picture on chat/completions with the image_generation built-in tool, then fetches the result with a second call on the same key and the same proxy exit. Only the prompt is forwarded; the rest is recorded as not forwarded, and the image is recorded as unpriced because no source publishes a per-image rate.

Uploads, edits and streaming

An edit is forwarded in the client's own encoding. A multipart upload goes out as multipart, streamed from the server's spooled copy of each file, and re-read from the start if the rail falls back to the next model. The JSON variant goes out as JSON. MEDIA_UPLOAD_MAX_MB sets an optional upload limit: above zero, a file larger than that many megabytes is refused with a 413 before any provider is asked, so nothing is spent on it.

A request that asks to stream is routed to a surface documented to stream it. When a rail has no such surface, a streamed image or speech request is answered as one event rather than a stalled stream.

What you see and what it costs

The Models page lists every media-rail model with its declared endpoints and media health, and each model publishes the fields its request takes as a JSON Schema per operation, each with who said so. That schema is shown only; nothing sent changes. Clients can read it from GET /v1/media/models . Analytics has a separate Media card, and every row is labelled by its own API, so a generated image reads as such in the requests table.

Media analytics: image, speech and video rows with their own cost figures, separate from the chat totals.

Media requests are priced like chat ones: a provider figure first, then models.dev, then LiteLLM when it is on, else unpriced. Generated media can optionally be stored, controlled by MEDIA_STORE_ENABLED .

The Models page names each model's kind, so a media model is offered on its rail and not to a coding agent.

Media tools for coding agents

MCC's media server, mcc-mcp , exposes one tool per filled rail plus a free status tool over MCP. It can be added to an agent from the Coding agents page, or written into Codex's config.toml , OpenCode's opencode.json and Command Code's mcp.json from the Desktop apps cards. The change is shown first, written only on confirmation, backed up once, and removable back to the same bytes. An entry MCC did not add is left alone. The server is off for every agent by default.

Configuration

The rails are MODEL_IMAGE , MODEL_TTS , MODEL_ASR and MODEL_VIDEO , each with a _FALLBACKS and _PAUSED list. The upload cap is MEDIA_UPLOAD_MAX_MB , optional storage is MEDIA_STORE_ENABLED , and the agent tools are gated by MCP_MEDIA_APPS . None of the rails is a chat tier: nothing on them is listed in /v1/models or offered to a coding agent.

Limits and behaviour

A model whose provider declares no endpoint for the operation is skipped uncharged and logged as unsupported.

A Mistral image fetch that fails after the host billed the picture fails the attempt, because the host has already charged it.

A media failure never benches a chat model; the rails keep their own health records.

An upload over the configured cap is refused before any provider is asked.

A field MCC cannot place on a translated surface is listed as not forwarded rather than silently dropped.

Providers: which hosts declare a media endpoint

Observability: media rows and media cost

Agents: the media server over MCP

Configuration: the media variables, names only

## Messaging surfaces for the local gateway
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/features/messaging/

Coding-agent sessions over Discord and Telegram

Messaging is optional. When it is on, a chat message becomes an inbound turn to a managed coding-agent session, and the reply comes back to the chat. It is the same proxy underneath, with the same routing, keys and log. It is optional and off by default. It is LLM messaging in its narrowest sense: a chat surface for a coding-agent session, over Discord or Telegram.

The messaging bridge is skipped entirely when the platform is none or when the selected platform's token is missing. Nothing else in MCC depends on it. When it is configured, an inbound message is normalised by the platform adapter, handed to one platform-agnostic workflow, and answered through an outbound messenger that queues sends, edits and deletes.

The Messaging page: the platform, its token fields, allowed channels or user IDs, an allowed directory and voice settings.

Discord

Create a bot in the Discord Developer Portal.

Enable Message Content Intent and invite it with read, send, message-history and Manage Messages permissions, so clear can remove user prompts.

Set Messaging Platform to discord .

Enter the Discord bot token, the allowed channels and an absolute allowed directory.

Apply the settings and restart the server if the page asks for it.

Telegram

Create a bot with BotFather.

Get your numeric user ID from userinfobot. In groups, grant the bot permission to delete messages.

Set Messaging Platform to telegram .

Enter the Telegram bot token, the allowed user ID and an absolute allowed directory.

Apply the settings and restart the server if the page asks for it.

An allowed directory is required and absolute, so a chat cannot be pointed at an arbitrary path by a message. The bot is the only ingress, and a chat that is not allowed is not served.

Commands

Usage

Behaviour

/stats

show session state

standalone /stop

cancel all work

reply with /stop

cancel only the selected request while other queued requests continue

standalone /clear

reset all MCC state and remove every tracked message in that chat, including user prompts, voice notes, MCC replies, Telegram's online notice and the clear command itself

reply with /clear

delete the selected message and its literal platform reply subtree, preserving its ancestors and siblings

The workflow keeps a per-chat generation and a global stop generation. A standalone stop invalidates every older provisional turn; a standalone clear invalidates only the invoking chat. Reply-scoped commands apply an exact reference transition, so a voice cancellation or an admitted tree wins without double-counting.

Voice notes

A voice note is downloaded, size-checked, transcribed and handed to the same inbound path as text. The transcription backend is chosen at install time: NVIDIA NIM, local Whisper on CPU or CUDA, or both. Local gated models need a Hugging Face key; NIM transcription needs the NVIDIA NIM key. Changing the credential an active voice backend uses requires a restart, while the same provider credential stays hot-replaceable when voice does not use it.

Install a voice backend (Linux, macOS or WSL)

curl -fsSL "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FiredMosquito831/my-claude-code/main/scripts/install.sh" | sh -s -- --voice-local

Pending voice notes have their own registry, which owns an optional status binding, cancellation by either message ID, and the exclusive handoff lease. A voice-transcribed stop or clear cannot cancel itself, and a stale flow cannot bind or remove a newer generation that reuses the same ID.

What you see

The Messaging page holds the platform, its token fields, the allowed channels or user ID, the allowed directory and the voice controls. The optional messaging step also appears in the Get Started checklist, so a new install is told it exists without being forced through it.

Get Started: messaging is one of the optional steps after the provider, the tier map and the agent.

Requests made through a messaging session are ordinary proxied requests and appear in Analytics like any other. The harness attribution names the agent behind them, so a chat-driven session can be told apart from a terminal one. A chat-driven request is not a special kind of request; it is the same proxy with a different ingress.

Analytics attributes each request to the coding agent harness that sent it, including sessions driven through messaging.

Configuration

The names are MESSAGING_PLATFORM , the platform token variables, MESSAGING_RATE_LIMIT and MESSAGING_RATE_WINDOW , and the voice settings for backend, device and model. A Telegram proxy URL is optional and used only for that transport. Values are configured on the Messaging page and written to the same .env the server reads; this site publishes no values.

Limits and behaviour

Messaging is off by default and skipped cleanly when it is not configured.

An allowed directory is required; a chat cannot widen it.

A voice note that fails transcription gets an error reply and is cleaned up; it does not leave a temp file behind.

A reply-scoped clear deletes only the selected subtree, never its ancestors.

The bridge is optional, but a request it makes is an ordinary request for routing, keys, cost and health.

Architecture: the session and request path

Agents: the sessions messaging drives

Observability: where a chat-driven request appears

Configuration: the messaging variables, names only

## Request log, analytics and cost with provenance
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/features/observability-and-cost/

The request log, analytics and cost with provenance

Every request through the proxy is logged, priced and searchable afterwards. That is what turns a router from a guess into a measurement: which model answered, which fallback spent the time, which key it cost, and where each price came from. This page is LLM observability and cost tracking in one place: the request log, the analytics and the source of every number.

The request log stores every completed request locally. It is searchable across prompt, reply, reasoning and tool calls, and it is the source of every number on the Analytics page: there is no second accounting system and no remote dashboard to reconcile against.

Analytics: stored requests, success rate, fallback share and token totals, over an all-time strip that keeps counting after stored rows roll over.

The log

One row per completed request carries its endpoint, harness, provider, key, model, status, turn, tokens, cost, time to first token and duration. A request that a local optimization answered records no provider, because none served it, and carries the rule and the prompt tokens no provider ever received. A hidden tab reads nothing.

The request log: provider, model, key, harness, tokens, reasoning, cost and latency for a range of requests.

A request's detail opens the attempts it walked, the key each one used, its timings, and the reasoning fields that went out. Raw diagnostics sit in five collapsed boxes below it: API payloads from both sides of the exchange, streamed events, the provider's raw output, API error tracebacks and CLI diagnostics, with a Raw or Normalized toggle. Every recorded line is shown a page at a time and never cut, and an empty box says which door or which setting is why.

One request expanded: its route attempts, the reasoning fields the router sent, and the fallback that answered.

Search and storage

The search index stores each distinct piece of text in its own file beside the log, so a search does not unpack every stored request. New requests are indexed as they are written; older ones are indexed when you press Build search index. The prompt chunk store keeps each repeated prompt part once, so turn N+1 of a conversation no longer stores turn N again. History is converted in the background, each prompt is read back byte for byte before it is replaced, and Pause and Continue sit beside the log's size.

The storage panel: the request log's size, its retention, and the controls that keep it bounded.

Retention is a cap, not a promise. REQUEST_LOG_ENABLED turns the log and Analytics on or off, and REQUEST_LOG_MAX_ROWS prunes the oldest rows periodically. Once the cap is reached the log is a rolling window, so All time means all time still stored, and counts stop rising rather than the dashboard being broken. The all-time strip below the stat cards is never pruned, so it keeps counting after stored rows roll over.

Analytics

Analytics is range-aware: any period you like, not just the presets, converted per boundary in your own timezone. It computes p50 and p95 latency, provider and model breakdowns, top errors and a failover panel that counts each primary-to-stand-in pair that fired. The wide-search cost of a query is said under the search box before you run it, as advice only: never narrowed, never refused, never truncated.

Model latency, p50 and p95, per model.

Failover: every primary-to-stand-in pair that actually fired, with its count, beside the statuses that caused them.

Cost with provenance

Each request is priced once, as it is logged, and the rung of the pricing ladder that answered each field is stored beside the number. The provider's own model list is the first rung; models.dev follows; the LiteLLM map is consulted when it is switched on; a cross-provider vote covers what remains. A request no source can price is stored as unpriced and shown as a dash, never as a fabricated zero.

The Cost panel: reported and estimated are two figures, never summed, and every total carries its priced denominator.

Honest totals are the rule here. A request whose cost was reported by a source and a request whose cost MCC estimated are shown side by side and never added into one number. Every total carries an N of M priced denominator so a partial figure cannot read as a complete one. Anthropic's 5-minute and 1-hour cache writes are recorded separately, and a 1-hour write is priced at a rate a source states, or shown as not priced with the reason; requests before the split keep their 5-minute price.

Exports and raw output

A JSON export covers whatever the filters currently select, and an attempt-level export writes one row per model the chain tried, not per request, so the fallbacks that spent the time are in the file too. Raw diagnostics can be exported in any of the same formats, and the Analytics export itself takes an opt-in Raw diagnostics field, off by default and bounded.

The provider's own bytes are available when you ask for them. With LOG_RAW_UPSTREAM_BYTES on, every chunk is kept exactly as the transport received it: stream comments, ID and retry lines, data prefixes, the done sentinel and in-band error frames all survive, and a refusal body is kept whole. It ships off, because raw output is the largest thing the log can hold.

The Token Optimizer

The Token Optimizer page shows what never reached a provider: tokens saved, rule fire counts and prompt-cache effectiveness. The local optimization rules that answer a request without a provider are listed there, and each request they answer records the rule and the tokens it saved.

The Token Optimizer: what never reached a provider, plus the opt-in trimming and RTK controls.

Limits and behaviour

Analytics is local-only, like the rest of the dashboard.

Every widget that aggregates history shows the window it covers; a chain from before a settings change is not read as the current config.

A read can never charge a key or bench a provider.

A request detail's empty diagnostic box names why it is empty rather than showing a blank panel.

Retention prunes the oldest rows; the all-time strip is the figure that survives it.

Architecture: how a request is priced and the rung stored

Architecture: the log, the index and the chunk store

Providers: the keys these costs are attributed to

Configuration: retention and log variables, names only

## Platform support: Windows, macOS and Linux
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/features/platform/

Platform, desktop app and updates

MCC runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, as a server, as a native desktop app, or both. There is one update path, one configuration directory and one set of commands, whichever route you took in. This page is the LLM gateway update path, and the platform support behind it: what the installer does on each system, and what it deliberately does not touch.

The server is the product; the desktop app is a window onto it. Every install route ends at the same server, the same dashboard and the same configuration directory. The server one-liners are the right choice on a headless box, a VPS, over SSH or inside WSL, where there is no tray to draw into.

Get Started: the same checklist in a browser tab or inside the desktop window.

What the installer does

Installs uv if it is missing, and replaces one below the required floor.

Installs Python 3.14 through uv, so no system Python is needed and none is used.

Downloads the latest release wheel and verifies the SHA-256 GitHub publishes for it.

Installs MCC into an isolated tool environment and puts every mcc-* command on your PATH.

Creates the configuration home, and with the desktop flag, installs the desktop app too.

The installer needs no Node, no Python and no git. It cannot install curl on Linux, macOS or WSL: it names the exact package-manager line for your machine and stops. On Windows it uses the built-in PowerShell, and the Command Prompt route passes the execution-policy flag a saved script would otherwise need.

After it finishes, close and reopen your terminal. The installer adds ~/.local/bin to your PATH, and a shell that was already open cannot see it. That is the single most common reason mcc-server looks missing straight after a successful install.

The desktop app and tray

The desktop app is a real window with its own icon and tray, not a second copy of the server. It has three server modes: spawn , where it starts the server; attach , where it connects to one already running; and off , where it does neither. It can start at login, and its preferences persist in the configuration home. The tray menu covers Open Admin, Check Server Status, Restart Server, the server mode, Start at Login, Tray Enabled, a Token optimizer submenu and Quit.

Its own prerequisites travel with its packages: the Windows installer bootstraps WebView2, the .deb declares its webkit dependency, and macOS needs nothing extra. WSL has no tray, and the app says so and refuses rather than pretending.

One update path

The dashboard shows the running version, announces releases and installs them with checksum verification. The installer is the same path: re-running it always fetches the newest release. An update is atomic. The new version is built beside the running one, run once to prove it works, and swapped in by two directory renames; if it never answers the health endpoint, the previous version is put back and started. The server is down for the stop, the rename and the start, not for the download and the dependency resolve.

A newer release is announced in the dashboard, with its changelog and a one-click update.

During an update the desktop window shows a stage timeline with timestamps, elapsed time and the installer's log tailed live. The progress document and the install log are written into the configuration home, so a failed update can be read afterwards.

The version panel: the running release and live status, in the dashboard sidebar.

Packaging

MCC ships as a Python wheel on PyPI, as an npm package that wraps the same digest-verified installer, and as native desktop installers for each platform. The npm route reads the machine before it installs anything: where there is a desktop session it also installs the native app, each verified against the release's checksum manifest; over SSH, in CI, on a headless box or in WSL without a display it installs the server alone and says why. The PyPI route is the one that assumes something: it requires Python 3.14 and provisions nothing for you.

Update and uninstall

Uninstall is one line, and it verifies every MCC command is gone before it reports success. The desktop app is removed separately, by the platform's own mechanism. A pre-6.40.0 install that lives in the legacy configuration home is migrated on first start by one atomic rename, nothing copied or merged, provided nothing is holding the directory open; mcc-migrate runs the same move by hand and refuses while it can see a live server.

Uninstall (Linux, macOS or WSL)

curl -fsSL "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FiredMosquito831/my-claude-code/main/scripts/uninstall.sh" | sh

Configuration

The install-time switches are flags, not settings: --dry-run , --version , --desktop , --no-restart , --no-start , --no-desktop and --yes-sudo . MCC_INSTALL_REF points the installer at a branch, and MCC_INSTALL_NO_START and MCC_INSTALL_NO_DESKTOP carry the same intent as environment variables. The server's own host and port are HOST and PORT .

Limits and behaviour

The Windows installer is unsigned, so SmartScreen asks for More info then Run anyway. Machines with Smart App Control on cannot run it; use the PowerShell one-liner there.

The macOS disk image is unsigned and quarantined, so moving the app across needs one quarantine-removal command. The server one-liner is never quarantined.

The installer cannot install curl, and it does not install Claude Code or any other agent.

Every other MCC server on the machine is listed and left running. A port held by something that is not MCC is reported rather than touched.

Quick start: install, first five minutes, update and uninstall

The CLI: the commands the installer puts on your PATH

The dashboard: the Update button and the version panel

Licence: AGPL-3.0-or-later or commercial

## 60 providers, keys and credential health
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/features/providers-and-credentials/

Providers, keys and credential health

Every provider MCC can route to is a card on one page. A card holds a key or a pool of keys, its rotation policy, its model list and its health. The rest of this page is what happens when a provider answers, refuses, or says nothing at all. Sixty LLM providers sit behind that one page, each with its own keys and its own health.

The provider table in the repository lists 60 cards across cloud APIs, subscription and OAuth sign-ins, gateways, local servers and marketplaces. MCC builds each model slug as <provider-id>/<exact-provider-model-id> , and free-text entry stays available when a provider cannot list its models.

The Providers page: a searchable card per provider, each badged Configured or Missing key and naming the setting that holds its key.

One key, or a pool

Put multiple API keys in one variable, comma-separated, and choose a policy with {ENV}_ROTATION . Every key in a pool gets its own upstream client and its own rate-limit window, so one key saturating or stalling never throttles the others. The order in the pool is the order the policies read.

Policy

Behaviour

single

always the first key; the default when one key is set

round_robin

spread requests across healthy keys in turn

least_used

the healthy key with the fewest requests goes first

failover / on_error

stick to the first healthy key until it fails, then move to the next; the default when several keys are set

Keys can be reordered without retyping the variable, and each key can carry a name. Names live in credential_names.json , keyed by a hash of the key and never by the key itself; they never reach an upstream request or the request log. A renamed key keeps its history, and two keys given one name read as the name plus their masked label.

Health is judged on the key, not on the weather

A key is only ever judged on signals about the credential. There are exactly three. A 401 or 403 walks an escalating lockout ladder of five minutes, one hour and one day, on its own counter. A 429 benches the (key, model) pair for exactly the wait the provider published, or a configured cooldown when it published none, and the key stays healthy for its other models. An exhausted-credit refusal, where the provider says in words that the account has no balance left, benches the whole key, because a wallet is not per model.

Credential health on Limits and Resilience: the two settings that can bench a key, and nothing else.

Everything else, including timeouts, 5xx, a 410 model-gone, other 4xx and transport faults, leaves every key untouched. A model that will not answer is the model's problem: the fallback chain moves to the next model instead of spending the pool on it. A timeout is explicitly not read as a broken socket, so a model that never answered is not charged against the rest of the pool.

Per-key performance on Analytics, with the provider diagnostics each key actually returned.

Custom providers and the model catalogue

Any other OpenAI-compatible endpoint can be added as a custom provider from the same page. A custom provider is not a second kind of provider: it is an ordinary descriptor injected from a different source. Its definition lives in custom_providers.json , never in the .env , because its static credential travels on the descriptor rather than through a settings field. Deleting a custom provider removes its refs from every route; disabling it leaves the refs and pauses them.

Custom provider cards: a base URL, a key pool and a measured reasoning dialect.

A custom provider cannot inherit its host's reasoning_effort vocabulary, so MCC measures it. At most two 16-token chat completions are sent, the first with a deliberately invalid effort value, and the enum is read out of the 400 the host answers with. The learned words are persisted and bound to a reasoning encoder exactly as a static provider declaration would be.

The Models page is the catalogue behind that: every model every configured provider publishes, with bulk visibility, capability probes, learned facts and an hourly background refresh. Each row names where its entry came from. Hiding a model changes what is listed, never what is routed.

The Models page: every model across every configured provider, each row naming the source its entry came from.

Learned facts: every negative this install taught MCC, shown with its evidence, expiring on a clock and forgettable per row.

OAuth sign-ins

An OAuth provider sits in the same grid and carries the same badges, but its credential is a sign-in rather than a string you paste. MCC supports a Claude subscription, ChatGPT and Kimi For Coding. The Claude subscription route is not permitted by Anthropic : Anthropic's published terms forbid routing Free, Pro or Max plan credentials on behalf of third-party users, and the risk is to your account. MCC limits it by admitting only Anthropic's own clients, using an attribution line that travels in the request body, and it documents the position rather than hiding it. Read docs/ANTHROPIC-SUBSCRIPTION.md before enabling it. The ChatGPT subscription has its own caveats and is documented in the same place.

InferHub is a marketplace, not an ordinary provider: a profile sets a price ceiling and MCC sends it on every attempt.

Proxy chains

A provider can go out through a named chain of proxy exits. A chain whose provider limits per address moves a refused or dropped request to another exit on the same model, within your switch limit, and remembers the refused exits across saves. A country refusal is about the address, not the key: it never locks a key out, on any route. Three ways to fill a chain are built in: a scan for a proxy you already run on this machine, a bring-your-own-tor card where each SOCKS port becomes one named identity, and VPN accounts, gateways and provider proxy lists. WireGuard files your VPN exports can be run by MCC as named loopback exits.

A proxy chain: named exits a request can move between on the same model, with their own keep-alive and recency controls.

Configuration

The provider credential settings are the environment variables named on the provider's card, for example ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , OPENROUTER_API_KEY or GEMINI_API_KEY . Rotation is {ENV}_ROTATION . The health knobs are CREDENTIAL_LOCKOUT_TIERS , RATE_LIMIT_COOLDOWN_SECONDS , RATE_LIMIT_COOLDOWN_MAX_SECONDS , RATE_LIMIT_COOLDOWN_MODE and CREDENTIAL_MODEL_BENCH_ESCALATION . Variables are named, never given example values.

Limits and behaviour

No bench duration is invented at the rotation layer: it comes from the provider's own Retry-After or the configured window.

A bare 402 that names no billing phrase rotates and falls through but charges nothing.

A key that fails 5xx or transport on every request is retried once per request rather than benched. That is the deliberate trade that stopped healthy keys being benched for faults they did not cause.

A custom provider's URL is called as typed; the generic profile deliberately does not normalise it.

Local providers (LM Studio, llama.cpp, Ollama) need a base URL rather than a key.

Architecture: the credential and health machinery

Routing: what a key is asked to serve

Configuration: the credential variables, names only

Glossary: rotation, bench, lockout, dial

## Reasoning control and output budgets per request
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/features/reasoning-and-budgets/

Reasoning control and output budgets

Every provider spells reasoning differently. MCC keeps one neutral policy, then lets each provider adapter translate only the subset its wire API can express. The same page also decides how long a model may think, how many tokens it may spend, and how long the router waits before it calls a silent model a failure. This page is LLM reasoning control and the output token budget that goes with it.

Reasoning is not one setting. It is three independent facts: whether the client wants reasoning on, off or by default; the named effort it asked for, when it named one; and an exact token budget, when it supplied one. MCC resolves those facts once, at the application boundary, and passes one immutable policy to the provider. Provider adapters alone decide how to spell it.

One scale, many dialects

When a numeric-budget provider needs a number, MCC expresses named effort through one product scale: minimal and low are 512 tokens, medium is 1,024, high is 2,048, xhigh is 4,096 and max is 8,192. An exact client budget takes precedence over the scale.

Each host declares a reasoning dialect: which fields it parses, the words it accepts in an effort field, whether it has an on/off channel, a numeric budget, an OFF spelling and an adaptive channel. A control is emitted only where the model has that knob and the host has a field to spell it in. Where one of the two is missing, the nearest thing both can express goes instead: an effort outside the host's vocabulary clamps to the nearest rung that host spells, and a toggle-only model on an effort-only host is sent the rung the client asked for, clamped to that host's enum. Where nothing can be expressed, nothing is sent, the model's own default applies, and the request log records that rather than implying an instruction was honoured.

Reasoning policy and route-specific overrides on Model Config, beside the local web-tool switches.

Adaptive reasoning on every door

ADAPTIVE is not an effort level and not a budget. It asks the host to think as much as it decides it needs, and each door says that in the host's own words: Anthropic's thinking: {"type":"adaptive"} verbatim; an on/off field switched on where that is a different field from its effort one; the highest rung the host publishes where effort is all it has, recorded as a substitution; and nothing at all where the host parses no reasoning field. Every request that does not ask for adaptive is byte-for-byte unchanged.

Learned rejections

A host that answers a 400 naming a reasoning field is retried once without that field, and on success the (provider, model) pair is remembered for the life of the process. The narrowing is instance-scoped: a configuration reload rebuilds the provider and forgets it. A complaint naming a sampling field is never treated as a reasoning rejection, and an unrecognised 400 still fails visibly.

Reasoning replay across turns

A coding conversation spans many turns, and each turn has to decide what to carry forward. MCC keeps that decision explicit per provider: native reasoning content, a native reasoning field, think tags, provider-specific chunks, or no replay. Turning computation off for the next generation does not silently erase prior assistant state a valid continuation needs.

Mechanism

Default

What it does

Encrypted reasoning replay

off

carries a Responses host's opaque encrypted item through your client's transcript and replays it only to the provider, endpoint, account and model that minted it; no readable reasoning text is written back

Carrier provenance guard

always on

refuses an MCC reasoning envelope at every door that cannot have minted it, and counts the refusal

Carrier text recovery

always on

where a Messages host signs nothing, keeps the readable summary and drops only the signature

Readable reasoning replay on Responses

on

replays an earlier turn's plain thinking text as a summary-only reasoning item, never as output text or a think tag

Parallel tool calls on Responses

on

asks a Responses host to batch independent tool calls into one turn

The provenance guard is the safety net. An envelope is host-bound: it is replayed only to the exact provider, endpoint, account and model that produced it. A request that carries an envelope into a door that cannot have minted it is refused and counted as history_carrier_foreign . Readable reasoning is untouched and still crosses models and providers.

Prompt-cache lifetime

Prompt caching is off by default: the client's own lifetimes go untouched. Set minutes per tier and MCC sends the host's nearest lifetime at least that long: 5 minutes or 1 hour on Anthropic and on Claude models through OpenRouter, in_memory or 24-hour retention on Azure OpenAI. Hosts that cache automatically, including ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Nous and NIM, get nothing. A per-provider or per-model row can override the lifetime, or force From client , for gateways that speak Anthropic's protocol.

Output budgets and deadlines

The output allowance is resolved separately from reasoning, and the order matters. When the resolved policy will ask the model to think, the ask is first raised to the model's own published output limit, because thinking and answer tokens are spent from one allowance the client sized for the answer alone. Then the model limit applies, then the unknown-default, then the floor, then the ceiling, then context headroom. The floor is the only step that raises, and it sits after the model limit so it can never ask for more than the model published, and before context headroom so it can never re-inflate a budget the remaining context cannot hold.

Limits and Resilience: output budgets, deadlines, chain benching, retries and credential health on one page.

Deadlines are the other half of a budget. A first-token deadline and a total deadline per route turn a silent model into a failure instead of a hang. The calculator shows what each model on your chains actually gets, which is rarely the number in the box, because the model limit, the floor, the ceiling and context headroom all interact.

The deadline calculator: what each model on your chains actually receives after every bound is applied.

Configuration

The reasoning policy and its per-tier overrides live on Model Config. The budgets and deadlines live on Limits and Resilience. The settings are named REASONING_* , MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS_* , REQUEST_*_DEADLINE* and PROMPT_CACHE_* ; the exact names and their purposes are on the configuration page. No example values are published for any secret-like setting.

Limits and behaviour

The router never uses the output-token limit as a reasoning budget. A named or numeric reasoning budget travels only through documented fields.

A provider-default intent emits no compute-control field at all.

An exact client token budget takes precedence over MCC's named-effort scale.

A reasoning control the host cannot express is not invented: nothing is sent and the request log says so.

Learned rejections are per process. A reload forgets them, deliberately.

Architecture: where reasoning is resolved in the request path

Routing: which model receives the policy

Configuration: the variable names behind these controls

Glossary: reasoning policy, dialect, carrier, budget

## Model routing and fallback chains for coding agents
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/features/routing/

Model tiers and fallback chains

A coding agent asks for a model by a name it knows. This page is LLM model routing: MCC turns that name into a real provider model, applies your reasoning and budget settings, and walks an ordered chain of stand-ins when the first cannot serve the request. The chain is yours, and every step is in the log.

Routing is the reason a proxy can be useful at all. Without it, every coding tool carries its own model list, its own keys and its own idea of what to do when a provider says no. With it, one tier map serves every tool, and swapping a model is one edit on one page.

What a request can name

The router accepts three forms. A direct provider model ref such as nvidia_nim/nvidia/model-name names the provider and the exact model. A gateway model ID is decoded by MCC's own ID codec. And the five coding-agent tier aliases are intercepted ahead of both: mcc/cyber , mcc/best , mcc/good , mcc/medium and mcc/cheap . They are pointers, not models. Each names one of the router's own global routes, together with that route's fallback chain and pause list.

A name that is not a direct ref or a tier alias is mapped by Claude tier. Names containing fable , opus , sonnet or haiku use the matching tier override when one is set, and otherwise fall back to MODEL . A blank MODEL_HAIKU follows MODEL , which is what a fresh install ships.

The tier map

Each tier has three settings: the model it routes to, an ordered comma-separated fallback chain, and a pause list. The dashboard renders them as one rail per tier, in the order the router walks them.

Five coding-agent tiers and their chains. A paused row keeps its place and is never tried.

A diagram of five tiers, each with a primary model and an ordered fallback chain, one row marked paused and the Haiku tier following the default model.

Six rails side by side, each with a primary model and up to ten numbered fallback rows. A struck-through row with an amber Paused badge keeps its place.

How a fallback chain behaves

The router resolves the requested tier to its primary model and records the route on the request.

The executor attempts the primary model with a healthy credential.

If the model rate-limits, errors or refuses, the next entry in that tier's chain is tried, then the next.

The first attempt that succeeds ends the walk. Every later entry is recorded as not reached.

The chain does not retry the same model forever. A 429 benches the (key, model) pair for the wait the provider published, and the key keeps serving its other models. An auth rejection locks that key out on an escalating ladder. A timeout, a 5xx, a 410 or a plain 400 is treated as the model's answer, and the chain moves to the next model instead of spending the rest of the key pool on it.

One request's ladder: a model sat out a rate-limit cooldown, another was paused, one answered, and the rest were never reached.

A request detail: the route attempts the router walked, the reasoning fields it sent, and the fallback that answered.

A walked chain with a recorded reason beside every model.

A diagram of a four-model chain where the first was in a rate-limit cooldown, the second was paused, the third answered and the fourth was never reached.

Pausing one entry

Each row on a rail has a Pause button. A paused model keeps its place and stays fully on screen, but the router never tries it: no attempt is spent, no deadline is consumed, and the request log lists it as not tried with the reason paused . Unlike most of the page, a pause is written the moment you click it, with no Apply, and the status panel offers an Undo. Pausing is per route: the same model paused on Opus keeps serving Sonnet.

Pausing is not hiding. Visibility changes on the Models page change what appears in /v1/models and never change routing; a pause changes routing and never changes listings. A route whose every model is paused fails with an error naming the key rather than quietly falling through to another route.

Per-agent tiers

A different agent can have a different tier map. MCC identifies the harness from the x-mcc-harness header or from the request's user-agent fingerprint, and resolves against that agent's override when one exists. The overrides live in harness_tiers.json , are parsed defensively and are cached on the file's own timestamp, so a dashboard write lands without a restart.

The vision adapter

An image request can be diverted to a model that can see, with its own chain. VISION_ADAPTER_MODE=describe adds a third behaviour for a blind tier: instead of dropping the image, MCC builds one ordinary routed plan per image over the vision chain, has a sighted model describe it, and sends the description onward. The description is cached on the image's content address, so a screenshot re-sent every turn is described once. Every failure returns to the behaviour the request would have had without the adapter: divert, or send the substitute image.

The vision adapter on Model Config, with its own rail and the describe-mode control.

Two image behaviours are automatic. Outbound pictures are resized to a 1568-pixel long edge on the router's own copy, never the client's. And an image a tool returns reaches the model as a picture rather than as base64 text: one walk finds an image or document inside a tool result, and the token estimator and the outbound converters call the same walk, so they cannot disagree about whether it is an image or 680,000 characters of text.

Where you see it

The tier map is on Model Config . The chain a request actually walked is on Analytics : the Failover panel counts every primary-to-stand-in pair that fired, and one request's detail shows each attempt with its key, timings and the reason it was or was not tried. The Models page lists what /v1/models advertises to clients.

Retries, credential health and rotation policies, which decide what a chain does between attempts.

Configuration

Routing is configured by names, not values. The tier models are MODEL , MODEL_MYTHOS , MODEL_FABLE , MODEL_OPUS , MODEL_SONNET , MODEL_HAIKU and MODEL_VISION . Each has a _FALLBACKS list and a _PAUSED list. The media rails use MODEL_IMAGE , MODEL_TTS , MODEL_ASR and MODEL_VIDEO , and are not chat tiers: nothing on them is listed in /v1/models or offered to a coding agent.

Setting

What it decides

MODEL

the model used when nothing more specific matches

MODEL_MYTHOS

Mythos-tier traffic, alias mcc/cyber

MODEL_FABLE

Fable-tier traffic, alias mcc/best

MODEL_OPUS

Opus-tier traffic, alias mcc/good

MODEL_SONNET

Sonnet-tier traffic, alias mcc/medium

MODEL_HAIKU

Haiku-tier traffic, alias mcc/cheap ; blank follows MODEL

MODEL_*_FALLBACKS

the ordered stand-ins walked after that route's model

MODEL_*_PAUSED

the entries kept in place but never tried

Limits and behaviour

Failover happens before the first streamed chunk. Once output has started, switching models would corrupt the response, so a mid-stream failure is surfaced to the client.

A request that carries no identifying harness resolves against the global chain. It is never failed for being unidentified.

Model Config: one rail per tier, with drag handles, Pause buttons and the Apply control that writes the .env.

Architecture: how the router and the chain are built

Reasoning and budgets: what is applied before an attempt

Providers and credentials: what a chain entry points at

Configuration: the settings named on this page

## Native web search and fetch proxy for any model
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/features/web-search/

The native web-search and web-fetch proxy

Claude Code's web_search and web_fetch are Anthropic server tools: normally Anthropic runs the search and bills you for it. MCC fulfils them at the proxy instead, against a provider you choose or a keyless fallback, and streams the result back as ordinary text. No Anthropic search credits are used, and it works with any model provider. It is a web search proxy and a web fetch proxy, in front of fifteen search backends.

A client emits a web_search tool-use block. MCC runs the search against the configured chain and returns the results as a regular text block, so a model that has never heard of the tool still receives useful text. The same shape covers web_fetch , which retrieves a page and returns its main content.

The Web Search page: route policy, provider cards with key health, the chain editor and advanced options.

Fifteen search backends

The search backends are DuckDuckGo (keyless), Ollama Web Search, Exa, Tavily, Brave Search, SearXNG, Jina Search, Serper, Firecrawl, Linkup, Perplexity Search, Parallel, SearchAPI.io, SerpAPI and Context7 for library documentation. WEB_SEARCH_PROVIDER accepts auto , off , disabled or one of those provider IDs.

Setting

Behaviour

auto

the first configured provider in catalogue order, never Context7; with no keys set it falls back to the keyless hops, so search works zero-config

off

only the keyless DuckDuckGo hop, without the provider registry

disabled

reject web searches without making an outbound search request

an explicit ID

pin that provider; missing credentials or an upstream failure are surfaced instead of silently changing providers

WEB_SEARCH_FALLBACK_POLICY controls how far the chain may move after the selected provider: auto , none , ddgs or legacy . Configuration failures such as a missing API key always fail visibly, DDGS is never attempted twice, and the rich digest names the provider that ultimately produced the results.

The search chain: a selected provider, then the keyless hops, with the provider named in the digest.

A diagram showing the selected search provider, the keyless ddgs metasearch and the keyless DuckDuckGo page hop, with fallback policies and zero-config behaviour.

The keyless DuckDuckGo hop

The last hop reads DuckDuckGo's HTML page first and its lite page only as a second try, with declared parser profiles and headers. Snippets are kept, ads are skipped, and your region and time window are respected through the DDGS_REGION and DDGS_TIMELIMIT settings. A bot check is reported as a rate limit rather than as no results, and optional spacing between requests is available, off by default.

Keys rotate like model keys

Every search service's keys follow the same rules as a model provider's keys: comma-separated pools, the same rotation policies, and the same health engine. The bench is shown in plain words with a Reset, and every key try is a row in Analytics. The chain itself is an ordered list of services with repeats, pause and drag, edited on the Search chain card.

The chain editor: an ordered list of search services with pause and reorder controls.

Web fetch

Web fetch returns the page's main content as markdown with links and tables: menus and footers are dropped. The extractor is loaded on the first fetch of a process, the output is capped at 24,000 characters and the marker names the extracted total, markdown is asked for in the Accept header, a Cloudflare challenge gets one honest retry, and a page served without a charset is read rather than refused. WEB_FETCH_EXTRACTOR=basic restores every earlier release's bytes.

Analytics

Web search has its own route and attempt analytics, with the captured input and output, separate from the chat log. That split matters because a search attempt is a different kind of call: it can fail on a key, on the query or on the search host, and the analytics keeps those apart from the model request that asked for it.

Web-search analytics: separate route and attempt analytics with the captured input and output.

Configuration

The route is WEB_SEARCH_PROVIDER and WEB_SEARCH_FALLBACK_POLICY . Each backend has its own key variable, named on its card. The keyless hop uses DDGS_REGION and DDGS_TIMELIMIT , and optional request spacing uses WEBSEARCH_LEGACY_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS . Web fetch uses WEB_FETCH_EXTRACTOR . Variable names only; no values are published.

Limits and behaviour

Context7 is never picked by auto: it answers with library documentation rather than web pages.

An explicit provider is strict by default; a missing key fails visibly instead of silently swapping to another backend.

The keyless hop is an unofficial metasearch and its engines may rate-limit an address. That is reported as a rate limit, not as an empty result.

Advanced options allow the model to receive full page text rather than snippets, restrict searches to specific sites, and set safe search, locale and freshness.

This is a server-tool proxy: a client that does not use the Anthropic server-tool shape is not affected.

Providers: the key pools and rotation this shares

Observability: where search requests are logged

Configuration: the search variables, names only

Glossary: server tool, chain, keyless hop

## Claude Code through a local LLM proxy
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/for/claude-code/

Claude Code through one local address

Claude Code is Anthropic's terminal agent, and it is one client here, not the frame around everything else. mcc-claude points it at My Claude Code on your machine, so the model behind its next request can be any provider you have configured, with a fallback chain and a priced log entry behind it. It is the Claude Code proxy setup in one command.

The command

Install Claude Code yourself, because MCC never installs an agent, then launch it through the proxy with one command:

Launch Claude Code against the local proxy

mcc-claude

The launcher sets the proxy address and the proxy token in the child process only, so nothing is written into your shell profile, your Claude Code settings or your own authentication. Every argument you pass is handed to Claude Code unchanged, which means the launcher is a drop-in replacement for the command you already type.

Add --discover-models to wire Claude Code's native /model picker to MCC's catalogue, which is built from the models your routes actually resolve to:

Launch with the native model picker wired to MCC's catalogue

mcc-claude --discover-models

A single prompt runs the same way, because -p is Claude Code's own flag: mcc-claude -p "summarise this diff" . mcc-claude-old keeps the earlier launch shape, which sets the full proxy environment and leaves auto-compact on.

What Claude Code gets

One address for every provider. Anthropic Messages traffic reaches whichever model your tiers resolve to, including a local server, without a second client configuration.

Fallback chains. When the first model cannot serve a request, the next rung is tried before the agent sees a failure, and each step is recorded.

Reasoning control and output budgets, translated once into each provider's own dialect rather than set per client.

Credential rotation and health, so a rate-limited key is benched and another key in the pool is tried for the same request.

A priced request log: which model answered, which key it used, how many tokens it spent and where the price came from.

The web tools, when the proxy's web-search setting is on. Claude Code's web_search and web_fetch are fulfilled at the proxy instead of by Anthropic.

What the launcher does not change

Your Claude Code installation, its settings files and its own authentication are untouched. The launcher sets environment variables for one process and exits with it, so a terminal that never ran mcc-claude is exactly the terminal it was before. If Claude Code is not installed, the launcher prints Anthropic's own install line and exits rather than installing anything on your behalf.

Where to go next

Every agent MCC can launch or configure

Quick start: install, run, and the first five minutes

Routing: tiers and fallback chains

Providers and credentials: what the request is routed to

## Codex CLI through a local LLM proxy
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/for/codex/

Codex CLI through one local address

Codex CLI is OpenAI's terminal agent, and it speaks the OpenAI Responses API. mcc-codex points it at My Claude Code on your machine, so the model behind its next request can be any provider you have configured, with a fallback chain and a priced log entry behind it. It is the Codex CLI proxy setup in one command.

The command

Install Codex CLI yourself, because MCC never installs an agent, then launch it through the proxy with one command:

Launch Codex CLI against the local proxy

mcc-codex

The launcher passes the proxy as an ephemeral -c assignment on the command line, so your own config.toml is never rewritten. The provider it declares is named for the proxy, points at the proxy's /v1 root, uses the Responses wire API and reads its key from an environment variable the launcher sets for that one process.

A single prompt runs the same way, using Codex's own subcommand: mcc-codex exec "summarise this diff" . mcc-codex resume --last continues the most recent session, and neither form needs a different launcher.

MCC also generates a model catalogue for Codex and points the launch at it, so the models Codex offers are the ones your routes actually resolve to, with the limits and prices the metadata ladder found.

The catalog is written under the MCC configuration home and named on the command line for that one launch, in the same way as the provider assignment. Nothing under your Codex home is rewritten, and a Codex session you start without mcc-codex sees exactly the configuration it saw before.

What Codex gets

One address for every provider, over the OpenAI Responses API that Codex already speaks.

Fallback chains. When the first model cannot serve a request, the next rung is tried before the agent sees a failure, and each step is recorded.

A generated model catalogue, so the models Codex lists are the ones your routes resolve to.

Credential rotation and health, so a rate-limited key is benched and another key in the pool is tried for the same request.

A priced request log: which model answered, which key it used, how many tokens it spent and where the price came from.

Per-agent attribution. The launcher marks the request as Codex's, so the log can name the agent behind it.

What the launcher does not change

Your Codex installation and its config.toml are untouched, because every assignment the launcher adds exists for one launch only. If Codex is not installed, the launcher prints OpenAI's own install line and exits rather than installing anything on your behalf.

Where to go next

Every agent MCC can launch or configure

Quick start: install, run, and the first five minutes

Routing: tiers and fallback chains

Providers and credentials: what the request is routed to

## Gemini CLI through a local LLM proxy
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/for/gemini-cli/

Gemini CLI through one local address

Gemini CLI is Google's terminal agent, and it speaks the Gemini API. mcc-gemini points it at My Claude Code on your machine, so the model behind its next request can be any provider you have configured, with a fallback chain and a priced log entry behind it. It is the Gemini CLI proxy setup in one command.

The command

Install Gemini CLI yourself, because MCC never installs an agent, then launch it through the proxy with one command:

Launch Gemini CLI against the local proxy

mcc-gemini

Gemini CLI publishes one variable for the endpoint, GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL , and it takes the proxy root with no /v1 and no /v1beta , because the SDK appends the model path itself. Setting that variable alone is not enough: Gemini CLI's own auth check refuses its gateway mode in a non-interactive run, so the launcher also writes one settings key into a document MCC owns and points Gemini CLI at it through its own GEMINI_CLI_SYSTEM_SETTINGS_PATH , in the child process only.

That document is merged as the system scope, so MCC's keys win while your own ~/.gemini/settings.json still supplies everything MCC does not name: your theme, your MCP servers, your memory. It is never written, never backed up and never read for authentication. The proxy token is not on disk either: GEMINI_API_KEY is read from the environment, and the launcher sets it for the child process only.

A single prompt runs with Gemini CLI's own flag: mcc-gemini -p "summarise this diff" , and -o json makes the same run machine-readable. Gemini CLI's own model picker lists Google's models only, so -m anthropic/<provider>/<model> is how MCC's routed models are reached.

What Gemini CLI gets

One address for every provider, over the Gemini API surface that Gemini CLI already speaks.

Fallback chains. When the first model cannot serve a request, the next rung is tried before the agent sees a failure, and each step is recorded.

MCC's routed models at -m , beside the Google models Gemini CLI lists itself.

Credential rotation and health, so a rate-limited key is benched and another key in the pool is tried for the same request.

A priced request log: which model answered, which key it used, how many tokens it spent and where the price came from.

Per-agent attribution. The launcher marks the request as Gemini CLI's, so the log can name the agent behind it.

What the launcher does not change

Your own ~/.gemini/settings.json and the OAuth tokens under ~/.gemini are untouched, because the launcher writes a separate document and the API-key path returns before the OAuth path is reached. If Gemini CLI is not installed, the launcher prints Google's own install line and exits rather than installing anything on your behalf.

Where to go next

Every agent MCC can launch or configure

Quick start: install, run, and the first five minutes

Routing: tiers and fallback chains

Providers and credentials: what the request is routed to

## OpenCode through a local LLM proxy
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/for/opencode/

OpenCode through one local address

OpenCode is an open-source terminal agent that reads its providers from a config file. mcc-opencode points it at My Claude Code on your machine, so the model behind its next request can be any provider you have configured, with a fallback chain and a priced log entry behind it. It is the OpenCode proxy setup in one command.

The command

Install OpenCode yourself, because MCC never installs an agent, then launch it through the proxy with one command:

Launch OpenCode against the local proxy

mcc-opencode

OpenCode reads its provider configuration from files rather than from arguments, so the launcher writes a config document of its own under the MCC configuration home and points the launched process at it through OpenCode's own OPENCODE_CONFIG variable. That variable names an extra config file that is merged into the precedence chain, so your opencode.json is never read, never written and never backed up.

The generated document names two environment variables rather than the token itself, and the launcher sets them in the child process only, so the proxy token is never on disk. A single prompt runs with OpenCode's own subcommand: mcc-opencode run "summarise this diff" .

mcc-opencode models mcc lists the models MCC published, with the limits and prices the metadata ladder resolved. mcc-opencode -m mcc/<provider>/<model> starts on one specific MCC-routed model. OpenCode 2, which installs beside v1 under its own binary, has its own launcher: mcc-opencode2 .

What OpenCode gets

One address for every provider, over the Anthropic Messages surface OpenCode already speaks.

Fallback chains. When the first model cannot serve a request, the next rung is tried before the agent sees a failure, and each step is recorded.

A generated model list with the limits and prices the metadata ladder resolved, reachable with models mcc .

Credential rotation and health, so a rate-limited key is benched and another key in the pool is tried for the same request.

A priced request log: which model answered, which key it used, how many tokens it spent and where the price came from.

Per-agent attribution. The launcher marks the request as OpenCode's, so the log can name the agent behind it.

What the launcher does not change

Your own opencode.json is untouched, because MCC writes a separate document and points one process at it. Stop launching through MCC and the file you wrote is the file you have. If OpenCode is not installed, the launcher prints its own install line and exits rather than installing anything on your behalf.

## Glossary of gateway and routing terms
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/glossary/

The words this product uses

MCC uses some ordinary words in a specific way. This page defines them once, from the product's own documentation, so a page elsewhere can use them without repeating the definition. It is the LLM gateway glossary: bench, chain, tier, rung, credential health and cost provenance, each defined once.

A — C

Adaptive reasoning

A request, spelled ADAPTIVE , that asks the host to think as much as it decides it needs. It is not an effort level and not a budget; each door says it in the host's own words, and a host with no reasoning field is sent nothing.

Bench

A time-bounded refusal to use a credential or a chain entry. A bench is scoped: a 429 benches a key and model pair, while an exhausted balance benches the whole key.

Budget

An exact output allowance, or the reasoning budget a client supplied. MCC keeps the two separate, and never uses an output limit as a reasoning budget.

Carrier

MCC's envelope for a Responses host's opaque encrypted reasoning item, carried through the client's own transcript. A carrier is host-bound: it is replayed only to the provider, endpoint, account and model that minted it.

Chain

An ordered list of stand-ins behind a route. A model listed twice is tried twice, and each listing is judged when it is reached.

Commit boundary

The moment the first protocol chunk is sent and the HTTP status can no longer change. A failure before it is an HTTP error; a failure after it is an in-band event.

Config home

The one directory that holds the .env, the request log and the documents beside them. It is ~/.mcc by default and is pinned by MCC_CONFIG_DIR .

Country refusal

A 403 that refuses the address rather than the credential. It never locks a key out, and the request still tries the next key, then the next model.

Credential pool

The comma-separated keys behind one provider, each with its own upstream client and rate-limit window, read in the order they are listed.

D — F

Dialect

The reasoning fields one host parses: an effort field and its words, an on/off channel, a numeric budget, an OFF spelling or an adaptive channel. A control is emitted only where the model has the knob and the host has the field.

Direct ref

A model named as provider/model , resolved without a tier. It is one of the three forms the router accepts, beside gateway IDs and tier aliases.

Door

One of the four protocol surfaces a client can enter: Anthropic Messages, OpenAI Responses, Chat Completions or Google Gemini. All four meet the same router.

Exit

One named address in a proxy chain. A refused or dropped request can move to another exit on the same model, within the chain's switch limit.

Failover

Moving from the route's primary model to a stand-in after a failure. It happens before the first streamed chunk; after that, the response is committed.

Fallback

One entry in a chain, or the act of walking the chain. A fallback can be paused, which keeps its place and never tries it.

G — I

Gateway model ID

A model identifier decoded by MCC's own gateway-ID codec, rather than a direct provider ref or a tier alias.

Generation

One provider-runtime snapshot with its own provider instances, limiters and quota state. A hot replacement publishes a new generation; old request leases drain against the one they started on.

Harness

The coding agent behind a request, identified from a header or the user-agent fingerprint. It drives per-agent tier maps and the request log's attribution.

Headroom

The context left after a prompt, which bounds how large an output allowance can be. It is applied after the floor, so it can lower a budget but never re-inflate one the context cannot hold.

InferHub

A marketplace provider that resells pooled accounts behind one key. A profile sets a price ceiling, and MCC sends it on every attempt so a request is never charged above it.

J — L

Key health

A key's state, decided only from signals about the credential: an auth rejection, a 429, or an exhausted balance. Timeouts, 5xx and other 4xx leave it untouched.

Keyless hop

The last search hop, which reads DuckDuckGo's HTML page and then its lite page without a key. It is unofficial and may be rate-limited, which is reported as a rate limit rather than as no results.

Learned fact

A negative this install taught the router, shown with its evidence, expiring on a clock and forgettable per row. A reasoning field a host refused is one example.

Lockout

The escalating bench for a key the provider keeps rejecting with an auth error: five minutes, one hour and one day by default, one step per consecutive rejection.

M — O

Media rail

One of the image, speech, transcription and video routes. A media rail walks its chain like a chat route but keeps its own health, and is never offered to a coding agent.

Model kind

What a model is for: chat, image, speech, transcription or video. A picker offers only its own kind, and a model whose kind is stated and is not chat is left out of the chat catalogue.

Model slug

The provider/model string MCC builds from the provider ID and the exact provider model ID. Free-text entry stays available where a provider cannot list its models.

No-thinking variant

A model-listing entry that forces reasoning off. It exists for compatibility, and the router treats the no-thinking name as a distinct route.

Optimization rule

A narrow local rule that answers a common low-value request before a provider is asked. A request it answers records the rule and the tokens no provider received.

OAuth provider

A provider whose credential is a sign-in rather than a pasted string: a Claude subscription, ChatGPT or Kimi For Coding. It sits in the same grid as a key-based provider.

Output allowance

The number of tokens a reply may use, resolved from the model, the route's ceiling and floor, context headroom and, when thinking is requested, the model's own published limit.

P — R

Provenance

The recorded source of a value. A price carries the rung that stated it; a claim on this site carries the path or command that proves it.

Provider card

One provider's entry on the Providers page: its badge, its key count, its rotation policy and its Configure and Refresh models controls.

Proxy token

The bearer token clients present to the proxy. It is generated for the machine on first start, and it is required once the host is not loopback.

Rail

A route rendered as a row on Model Config: a primary model and its ordered fallbacks. A media rail is the same shape for a media endpoint.

Rate-limit window

One key's own quota state. Every key in a pool has its own, so one key saturating or stalling never throttles the others.

Request log

The local SQLite record of every completed request, with its attempts, tokens, cost and latency. Analytics is computed from it; it is not a second accounting system.

Rotation

Choosing which key in a pool serves a request: single, round robin, least used or failover. Rotation is per pool, and each key's order is the order the policy reads.

Rung

One step of a resolution ladder, such as the pricing ladder or the metadata ladder. A value records the rung that answered it, so two surfaces cannot disagree about its source.

S — U

Safety classifier

Claude Code's narrow auto-mode prompt shape. It is a routing policy, not a short-circuit: MCC forces reasoning off so the client receives a parser-readable verdict.

Search chain

An ordered list of search services with repeats, pause and drag. It is walked at the proxy, and its keys follow the same rotation and health rules as a model key.

Server tool

A tool the protocol expects the server to run, such as web search or web fetch. MCC fulfils it at the proxy instead of sending it upstream.

Subscription window

A plan's usage limit with its reset time, as a provider reports it. A window and a cash balance are two blocks and never one total.

Tier

A coding-agent route such as Fable, Opus, Sonnet or Haiku, mapped to a real model and a chain. A tier alias is the protocol name for one of those routes.

Tier alias

One of mcc/cyber , mcc/best , mcc/good , mcc/medium , mcc/cheap or mcc/vision . It is a pointer to a global route, not a model.

Token optimizer

The page and the opt-in RTK integration that show what never reached a provider: tokens saved, rule counts and prompt-cache effectiveness.

Tuning

A parameter set for the shared rotation engine. The provider tuning excludes the generic cooldown ladder; the web-search tuning keeps it, because a search key that keeps erroring is worth resting.

V — Z

Vision adapter

The route that diverts an image request to a model that can see. In describe mode, a sighted model describes each image and the description is cached on the image's content address.

Wire capture

The recorded message and tool structure actually sent, bounded and inspectable. It is what lets a reasoning adaptation appear in the request detail.

## Licence: AGPL and the commercial option
https://myclaudecode.danubelabs.net/license/

The exact terms

My Claude Code is dual-licensed. The free option is the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3 or later. The other option is a commercial licence, negotiated case by case. This page states what each one means; it is not legal advice. The free option is AGPL-3.0-or-later; the other is a commercial licence agreed in writing.

Licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 or later (AGPL-3.0-or-later), or a commercial licence by negotiation.

The AGPL option

The AGPL option is free and open source, and it is open to everyone. Personal use, study, modification, and commercial use are all permitted at no cost, including running the proxy for your own work or for your employer's work. What the AGPL asks in return is source code: if you convey the software, or run a modified version of it as a network service that other people interact with, you must offer those users the complete corresponding source of your version under the same licence. Section 13, Remote Network Interaction, is the clause that extends that duty to network use.

The Required Notice at the top of the licence file must be preserved. That is a term of the AGPL grant, stated under the additional term of AGPL section 7(b):

Required Notice

Copyright (c) 2026 FiredMosquito831
https://github.com/FiredMosquito831/my-claude-code

The commercial option

The commercial licence releases you from the AGPL's source-sharing obligation. It is the right choice if you want to offer the software, or a work based on it, as a hosted or managed service; route model or API traffic commercially through it as part of a paid product; reuse its code, its routing logic or its algorithms inside a product you ship without publishing that product's source under the AGPL; or distribute it inside a closed-source appliance, gateway or bundle.

A commercial licence is the only way to use the software outside the terms of the AGPL. There is no other exception, standing permission or informal allowance. Terms are negotiated case by case: scope, duration, support expectations and price depend on what you are building. There is no published price list and no click-through agreement; every commercial licence is a written agreement with the author.

The inherited MIT portion

The model-routing infrastructure of this project is derived from the MIT-licensed Free Claude Code by Ali Khokhar (Alishahryar1), whose notice is reproduced in the licence file. Substantial portions of that original work remain in this project, and the MIT terms continue to apply to them. The inherited upstream code stays under its original MIT licence in every case: a commercial licence changes the terms of the author's own work, not of that inherited portion.

Trademarks and non-affiliation

My Claude Code is an independent open-source project. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or OpenCode. Claude is a trademark of Anthropic; Codex and ChatGPT are trademarks of OpenAI; Gemini is a trademark of Google. Other marks are their owners'. Provider names are used to describe what the software connects to, not to claim any relationship.

What this page is not

It is not legal advice.

It is not a licence in itself. The licence is the full text in the repository's licence file; a commercial licence exists only once it is agreed in writing.

It does not relicense any provider's terms. Your use of a model or an API is governed by that provider's own agreement.
